meta.name: Meridian
meta.title: SDE-2 and applied AI preparation desk
meta.hours: About 12–18 hours a week. Use the 60-minute cut when life is smaller, and the 3-hour cut when you can go deep.
meta.level_note: SDE-2 usually sits near Google L4, Meta E4, Amazon L5, and Microsoft 62. Ladders move. Confirm the requisition.

paths.name: General SDE-2
paths.for: Google L4, Meta E4, Amazon L5, Microsoft 62, and similar product-engineering loops.
paths.weekly_shape: About 70% coding and design, 20% CS and stories, 10% AI literacy plus one small project so you are not lost if the conversation turns to models.
paths.daily_rule: Protect the coding block. On AI-heavy days, do the 60-minute cut of the AI work and spend the rest on a second problem.
paths.risk: Treating system design as box-drawing, and treating behavior as optional. L4 rejects often come from communication and shallow design, not from missing a rare algorithm.

paths.name: SDE-2 on an AI product team
paths.for: Teams shipping search, assistants, support bots, ranking, or internal LLM tools inside big companies.
paths.weekly_shape: About 45% coding, 25% design, 30% applied AI. The RAG project is part of your loop, not a side hobby.
paths.daily_rule: Do both blocks. If time collapses, keep one timed problem and the AI drill. Do not drop retrieval eval to watch another framework video.
paths.risk: Collecting libraries (LangChain, LangGraph, three vector databases) without a metric. Interviewers ask what you measured.

paths.name: Applied AI engineer who still has a coding screen
paths.for: AI-titled roles that still run data structures rounds, plus startups where the onsite is a practical build plus one coding screen.
paths.weekly_shape: About 35% coding maintenance after Week 8, 15% classic design, 50% building and evaluating. Do not skip Weeks 1–8. Applied roles still reject on basic coding.
paths.daily_rule: After Week 8, you may shorten new patterns and lengthen the build. Before Week 8, follow the coding block as written.
paths.risk: A demo that hallucinates confidently, or a coding screen you postponed until the week of the interview.

rules: One interview language. Python is the best default if the AI track matters. Java or Go if a specific team writes the screen in that language and you already have fluency.
Every coding session uses the checklist card. Untimed exploration is allowed only when learning a pattern for the first time, and it still ends with one timed attempt.
File problems by pattern trigger, not by the website's chapter.
Spaced review: the next day, the Sunday of that week, and once more the following Sunday if confidence was below 4.
Mocks start in Week 7, not in Week 16. A mock without a written retro does not count.
The AI project is cumulative. Week 13 extends Week 12. Do not restart in a new framework.
Loops change. The company sheet is a prior, not a contract. Ask the recruiter what your loop contains in the week you schedule it.
Level names differ. Google L4, Meta E4, Amazon L5, and Microsoft 62 are the usual SDE-2 neighborhood, and postings still need to be read.
Do not invent stories, metrics, or employers. A smaller true story beats a cinematic false one. Interview loops compare details.
Compensation numbers go stale. If you are negotiating, check a current public source the same month and treat it as a range, not a promise.

This plan is about sixteen weeks at roughly twelve to eighteen hours a week. If you have less time, follow the 60-minute column and let the calendar stretch. If you have more, use the 3-hour column. Do not add extra topics outside the library until the gap list in Week 16 says so.
Rest is in the plan. The Sunday rows are lighter on purpose.

weeks.title: Make the language boring
weeks.intent: Skip this week only if you can write functions, hash maps, classes, and recursion in your interview language without looking anything up. Everyone else starts here. Pick one language and do not switch: Python if you also want the AI track, Java or Go if a target team publishes in that language.
weeks.exit: You can solve four easy array or hash problems in one sitting, narrating time and space, without tutorial tabs open.
weeks.dsa: Syntax, collections, recursion, reading a prompt.
weeks.systems: None yet. Set up a notes repo.
weeks.ai: Install Python, a notebook or script runner, and pin one model API key in an env file you do not commit.
weeks.behavior: Inventory projects for later stories. Do not polish a resume yet.
weeks.rhythm: 90 minutes of code, 20 minutes of notes. No new frameworks.
weeks.resources: Your language's official tour. A blank repo named interview-notes.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.theme: Pick the language and the notebook
days.coding: Write a one-file cheat sheet from memory: variables, if, for, while, functions, list/array, dict/map, set, class with one method. Anything you cannot write, study, then rewrite from a blank file.
days.problems: No LeetCode. Build: word count from a string, using a map.
days.second: Create the notes repo with folders: patterns, stories, systems, ai, mocks. Add a README that states your target level (SDE-2 / Google L4 or equivalent) and your interview language.
days.drill: Close every doc and retype the class-and-map example.
days.review: List five projects you have actually shipped or studied. One line each.
days.min60: Retype the map word-count from a blank file.
days.hrs3: Add tests for empty input, repeated words, and punctuation. Read your language's style guide for one hour.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.theme: Complexity while the code is still small
days.coding: For word count, nested-loop duplicate search, and binary search, write time and extra space before running. Define O, Θ, and Ω in your own words. State one amortized example: dynamic array append.
days.problems: Contains Duplicate, brute force then hash set.
days.second: Write the rule you will use in interviews: brute force first in speech, then the better structure, then code the better one if you can still finish.
days.drill: 90-second explanation of why the hash set is expected linear time.
days.review: Add a Patterns note: hash set = expected O(1) membership.
days.min60: Contains Duplicate plus the spoken complexity.
days.hrs3: Time both solutions on 100k integers and write what the clock did versus what Big-O promised.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.coding: Trace factorial and a list sum on paper with the call stack. Then write them. Identify the base case before the recursive case, every time.
days.problems: Fibonacci recursive, then with a memo dict. Climbing Stairs only if Fibonacci felt easy.
days.second: Draw how a call stack maps to a stack data structure. You will need this for DFS and for reading traces.
days.drill: Say the base case out loud before writing any recursive function today.
days.review: Note the two bugs you hit (missing base, wrong argument) in a 'bugs I repeat' list.
days.hrs3: Rewrite Fibonacci bottom-up. Compare stack depth versus table size.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.theme: Read a prompt like a contract
days.coding: Take one easy array problem. Before code: restate, list inputs and outputs, name three examples including empty and single-element, name the brute force, then code.
days.problems: Two Sum. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock.
days.second: Start a mistake log with columns: problem, bug, pattern, rule. You will fill this for sixteen weeks.
days.drill: Write three examples before the editor, even if you 'already know' the problem.
days.review: File Two Sum under hash map, not under arrays.
days.min60: Two Sum with examples written first.
days.hrs3: Solve both problems again on paper, no IDE. Time each at 25 minutes.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.coding: Add a tiny test function to yesterday's solutions. Step through one failure with a debugger or print-traces you planned, not random prints.
days.problems: Valid Anagram. Rewrite it with a fixed-size count array if the alphabet is known.
days.second: Write your interview checklist on one card: clarify, examples, brute, optimize, code, test with the examples, then one extra edge.
days.drill: Name the edge case before you run the test.
days.review: Add 'known alphabet → count array' to Patterns.
days.min60: Valid Anagram plus the checklist card.
days.hrs3: Practice the checklist on Group Anagrams at an untimed pace. Stop at 40 minutes and read a clean solution if stuck.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.coding: Four easy problems, 25 minutes each, interview language only. Stop when time ends even if unfinished. Tag each: solved clean / solved messy / hint / unread.
days.problems: Choose from: Contains Duplicate, Valid Anagram, Two Sum, Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, Valid Palindrome, Invert Binary Tree only if you already know tree syntax.
days.second: If two or more were unread, repeat Week 0 next week and do not start Week 1. That is a decision, not a delay.
days.drill: Score the set with the four tags. No new study after the fourth timer.
days.review: Write the one pattern that felt least fluent.
days.hrs3: Redo the messy ones untimed and write a five-line postmortem.

days.week_title: Make the language boring
days.theme: Rest, notes, and a story seed
days.coding: No new problems. Re-read Patterns.md and the mistake log. Retype one solution you marked messy.
days.second: Draft story seed 1 in four lines: a bug or outage you touched, what you owned, what changed, what you would do differently. Messy is fine.
days.drill: Retype one solution from memory.
days.review: Close the laptop after the retype. Sleep is part of recall.
days.min60: Retype the messy solution. Skip the story if you are exhausted; add it tomorrow morning.
days.hrs3: Expand the story seed to half a page. Read one page of your language's standard library for the collections you will use.

weeks.title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
weeks.intent: Build the hash-map reflex and a truthful mental model of a language model. SDE-2 loops assume both fluency with linear structures and, on AI teams, the ability to talk about models without mythology.
weeks.exit: You can pick the right map or set structure in the first five minutes of an array or string problem, and you can explain token, context, and sampling without notes.
weeks.dsa: Arrays, strings, hash maps, sets, prefix sums, frequency counts.
weeks.systems: None. Keep the checklist card visible.
weeks.ai: Tokens, context windows, temperature and top-p, why the model is not a database.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 2: a time you made a tradeoff under incomplete information.
weeks.rhythm: 75 minutes coding, 30 minutes AI literacy, 15 minutes notes. One timed medium by Friday.
weeks.resources: NeetCode array and hashing section, or the Blind 75 array cluster. Any current chat-model API reference for sampling parameters. Karpathy's 'Intro to LLMs' talk for the mental model, one sitting.

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.theme: Hash maps are the default tool
days.coding: Solve from the checklist: restate, examples, brute, then map. Say expected time and the collision caveat in one sentence.
days.problems: Two Sum. Valid Anagram if Week 0 was skipped.
days.second: AI: write six sentences. A language model predicts a next token. It was trained to continue text. It does not look up your company wiki unless you give it tools or retrieved text. Temperature reshapes randomness. A context window is a hard budget.
days.drill: Spoken: 'I will store value → index so the complement is a lookup.'
days.review: Patterns: complement map. Mistake log if you used a nested loop past the brute sketch.
days.min60: Two Sum plus the six AI sentences.
days.hrs3: Group Anagrams. Then read the sampling section and add temperature, top_p, and max tokens to a glossary file.

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.coding: Count, then bucket or sort the counts. Know when a heap is optional versus when a bucket sort is enough because the count is bounded by n.
days.problems: Top K Frequent Elements. Group Anagrams.
days.second: Embeddings preview, still conceptual: a word or sentence can be a list of numbers. Similar meaning, nearby lists. You will build this in the AI weeks. Today, only write the definition of cosine similarity in words.
days.drill: State why bucket sort by frequency is O(n) after the count.
days.review: Patterns: frequency map, then bucket by count.
days.min60: Top K Frequent Elements only, with the spoken complexity.
days.hrs3: Implement cosine similarity for two tiny lists in plain Python. No libraries. Compare [1, 0] and [0.9, 0.1].

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.theme: Strings and two pointers, first pass
days.coding: Opposite-ends pointers for palindromes and pair sums on sorted data. Same-direction pointers come next week; do not force them today.
days.problems: Valid Palindrome. Two Sum II on a sorted array.
days.second: Prompting versus training: a prompt is input in the context window. Training changes weights and is expensive. Write three prompt rules you will actually use: role, constraint, example. Note that a clever prompt does not fix missing facts.
days.drill: Draw the pointers on paper for one palindrome case before coding.
days.review: Patterns: sorted input → two pointers before a hash map.
days.hrs3: 3Sum only to the point of the sorted + skip-duplicates plan. If the code is not clean in 40 minutes, stop and write the plan in words.

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.coding: Build the prefix array, then answer range sums in constant time. Watch the off-by-one at the left boundary. Subarray sum equals k is the hash-map cousin: store prefix counts.
days.problems: Range Sum Query Immutable, or implement it yourself. Subarray Sum Equals K.
days.second: Context limits in practice: paste a long article into a model and ask for a detail from the middle and from the end. Note what it drops. This is 'lost in the middle', which you will meet again in RAG.
days.drill: Explain the prefix-count map for Subarray Sum Equals K in four sentences.
days.review: Patterns: prefix sum; prefix frequency map.
days.min60: Implement range sum and explain the off-by-one.
days.hrs3: Finish Subarray Sum Equals K timed at 35 minutes, then write the lost-in-the-middle observation.

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.coding: When the problem says constant extra space, look for swaps, two pointers, or writing back into the same array. Do not allocate a second copy out of habit.
days.problems: Move Zeroes. Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array. Product of Array Except Self.
days.second: Write a one-page glossary from memory: token, context window, temperature, top-p, hallucination, prompt, weight, inference. Look up only the ones you cannot define.
days.drill: Product of Array Except Self: explain the left-product and right-product passes without division.
days.review: Patterns: left/right pass when division is banned.
days.min60: Product of Array Except Self explanation, then code if time remains.
days.hrs3: Timed 40-minute medium from this week that you have not touched. Then fill glossary gaps.

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.coding: Three problems, 35 minutes each. New or redo. Stop at the timer. Tag clean, messy, or stuck.
days.problems: Longest Consecutive Sequence. Top K Frequent Elements redo if messy. A fresh Group Anagrams variant from your list.
days.second: No new AI chapter. Add five lines to the glossary only if a term shook loose while you were coding.
days.drill: One clean medium. Stop even if the second is unfinished.
days.review: File each problem under its pattern, not under the website's chapter name.
days.min60: Longest Consecutive Sequence, tested with empty and one-element inputs.
days.hrs3: Full three-problem set plus a short written postmortem: where the checklist was skipped.

days.week_title: Arrays, hashing, and what an LLM is doing
days.coding: Redo one stuck problem untimed, from a blank file. No new pattern.
days.problems: The stuck problem from yesterday only.
days.second: Story seed 2: a tradeoff with incomplete information. Four lines: situation, what you chose, what you gave up, what happened.
days.drill: Blank-file redo of one problem.
days.review: Walk once. Do not add a new topic on Sunday.
days.min60: Blank-file redo. Save the story for a fresh Monday if you are tired.
days.hrs3: Expand story seed 2. Skim your glossary and mark three terms you still cannot teach.

weeks.title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
weeks.intent: Sliding window and monotonic stacks show up constantly. This week also makes embeddings physical: small vectors, a similarity function, a ranked list.
weeks.exit: You can recognize a variable window versus a fixed window in the first read, and you can rank three short texts by cosine similarity with code you wrote.
weeks.dsa: Sliding window, two pointers same direction, stack, queue, monotonic stack.
weeks.systems: Sketch a stack frame. Still no distributed systems.
weeks.ai: Vectors, dot product, cosine, a tiny ranking script.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 3: a disagreement with a teammate.
weeks.rhythm: One pattern in the morning, one small AI script on three days, timed set on Saturday.
weeks.resources: NeetCode sliding window and stack. A 30-line Python script is enough for vectors; do not install a vector database yet.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: Fixed size k: add the new right element, remove the element that fell out on the left. Keep a running sum or count so you do not rescan.
days.problems: Maximum Average Subarray I. Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K, if you have it in your list; otherwise implement the sum version yourself.
days.second: Represent three sentences as bags of word counts (tiny vectors over a shared vocabulary). Rank them against the query 'payments failed at checkout' using the cosine you wrote in Week 1.
days.drill: State the add/remove invariant before coding.
days.min60: One fixed-window problem plus a spoken invariant.
days.hrs3: Finish the ranking script and print scores. Write why bag-of-words misses the synonym 'declined' for 'failed'.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: Grow right until the window is invalid, then shrink left until it is valid. Decide whether you want the longest or the shortest valid window before you code.
days.problems: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Longest Repeating Character Replacement.
days.second: Read one page on embeddings from a current vendor doc or a textbook chapter. Write the difference between a bag-of-words vector and a learned embedding in five lines.
days.drill: Say 'longest' or 'shortest' before the first line of code.
days.min60: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters only.
days.hrs3: Minimum Window Substring as a stretch. Stop at 40 minutes and write the need/have counter plan if the code is wrong.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: A stack is the right tool when the last unmatched open thing must close first. Draw the stack for one nested example.
days.second: Call three embedding API texts or, if you have no key, use a local sentence-transformers model only if install is painless. If neither is available, keep yesterday's bag-of-words and write down what an API would have changed. Do not spend the day on install drama.
days.concept: Embedding call or a written substitute
days.drill: Valid Parentheses on paper, then code.
days.review: Patterns: stack of opens; stack of values plus stack of minimums.
days.hrs3: Min Stack and a note on O(1) getMin. Record whether you used a real embedding or the substitute, and why.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: Maintain a stack of indices in decreasing or increasing order of values. When a new value breaks the order, resolve the answers for the indices you pop.
days.second: Write a failure note: keyword overlap is not meaning. Your bag-of-words ranker can be fooled by a sentence that repeats 'payments' in an unrelated way. Learned embeddings reduce that and introduce their own failures.
days.drill: Daily Temperatures: explain one pop in words.
days.hrs3: Daily Temperatures timed 30 minutes. Add the lexical-versus-semantic note to the AI folder.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: Implement a queue using two stacks, or use the language deque correctly. Then do one BFS on a binary tree if tree syntax is available; otherwise wait until Week 4 and do Number of Recent Calls instead.
days.problems: Implement Queue using Stacks. Number of Recent Calls.
days.second: No new model theory. Draw the pipeline you will build later: text → embedding → nearest neighbors → answer. Label which box you have already touched (embedding and cosine).
days.drill: Explain amortized O(1) for the two-stack queue.
days.review: Patterns: deque for sliding window maximum, preview only.
days.hrs3: Sliding Window Maximum as stretch, monotonic deque. Pipeline sketch labeled with 'done' and 'later'.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: Three timers, 35 minutes. At least one window and one stack.
days.problems: Minimum Window Substring or Longest Repeating Character Replacement. Daily Temperatures redo. A new medium you have not seen from this cluster.
days.second: Freeze AI features. If the ranker script is uncommitted, commit it with sample output in the README.
days.drill: One medium, tested.
days.review: Postmortem: did you name longest versus shortest before coding?
days.hrs3: Full set plus commit. Write the three invariants you can now say without notes.

days.week_title: Windows, stacks, and a first feel for vectors
days.coding: Blank-file redo of the messiest problem. No new pattern.
days.second: Story seed 3: a disagreement. What did you believe, what did they believe, how did it resolve, what was the user impact. Avoid villain narratives.
days.drill: One redo.
days.hrs3: Half-page story. List stack problems that are actually recursion in disguise.

weeks.title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
weeks.intent: Linked lists punish sloppy pointer handling. Binary search punishes sloppy bounds. The AI block this week is a whiteboard transformer: names and data flow, not a derivation of every matrix.
weeks.exit: You can reverse a list and search a rotated array without off-by-one panic, and you can draw query, key, and value on one page.
weeks.dsa: Linked lists, fast and slow pointers, binary search, search on the answer.
weeks.systems: Pointer diagrams. Memory: stack versus heap at interview depth.
weeks.ai: Attention, QKV, residual, layer norm — names and roles.
weeks.behavior: None new. Tighten story seeds 1–3 to half a page each if they are still scraps.
weeks.rhythm: Draw before you code on list and search days.
weeks.resources: NeetCode linked list and binary search. The illustrated transformer articles are enough; do not start a training run.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: Draw nodes and arrows. Write the dummy-head version and the in-place reverse. Update the arrow before you lose the rest of the list.
days.problems: Reverse Linked List. Merge Two Sorted Lists.
days.second: Draw a single transformer block from memory after a short read: input, attention, add-and-norm, feed-forward, add-and-norm. Label residual as 'keep a path for the original signal'.
days.drill: Reverse a three-node list on paper, then code.
days.review: Patterns: dummy head; reverse by rewiring next.
days.hrs3: Merge Two Sorted Lists and the block diagram from memory a second time at night.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: Floyd cycle detection. Middle of the list. Do not convert the list to an array unless the interviewer allows it and you say the space cost.
days.problems: Linked List Cycle. Middle of the Linked List. Reorder List if the first two are clean.
days.second: Attention in one paragraph: each token looks at the others and takes a weighted sum of their values. Weights come from query-key similarity. You do not need softmax algebra yet; you do need the sentence.
days.drill: Explain why slow and fast meet if there is a cycle.
days.review: Patterns: fast/slow for cycle and middle.
days.min60: Linked List Cycle explanation plus code.
days.hrs3: Reorder List. Write the Q, K, V roles in your own words under the diagram.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: Pick one bound style and keep it: while low <= high, or while low < high. Draw the mid calculation and the discarded half. Watch overflow if you use (low+high)/2 in Java; in Python it is a style point, not a bug.
days.problems: Binary Search. Search Insert Position. First Bad Version or a lower-bound implementation.
days.second: KV cache, name only: during generation the model reuses past keys and values so it does not recompute the whole prompt every token. You should know why streaming feels token-by-token.
days.drill: Say which half you discard and why, for one example.
days.review: Patterns: lower bound versus exact search.
days.min60: Implement lower bound and test it.
days.hrs3: Search in Rotated Sorted Array. Add the KV-cache sentence to the glossary.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: When you can check 'is X enough?' monotonically, binary search the answer. The search space is not the array index.
days.problems: Koko Eating Bananas. Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days, or a simpler feasibility check you write yourself.
days.second: Write three interview sentences you can say if asked 'how does a transformer differ from an RNN?': attention sees the whole context in a layer, training parallelizes over positions, long context is still expensive.
days.drill: State the monotonic check in words before coding.
days.review: Patterns: binary search on a feasibility predicate.
days.min60: Koko Eating Bananas, predicate written in a comment first.
days.hrs3: A second feasibility problem. Practice the three sentences out loud.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: Find which half is sorted. If duplicates are allowed, know that the worst case degrades and say so.
days.problems: Search in Rotated Sorted Array. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.
days.second: No new architecture. Redo the transformer diagram from a blank page in ten minutes.
days.drill: Find Minimum, with the sorted-half argument spoken.
days.min60: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.
days.hrs3: Both rotated problems timed. Diagram from memory. Note the duplicate-element caveat.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: Three timers. One list, one search, one redo.
days.problems: Reverse Linked List redo if needed. A rotated search. Koko or lower bound.
days.second: Commit the diagram as a photo or a text sketch in the notes repo.
days.drill: One timed search problem, bounds checked.
days.review: Log every off-by-one. They are the actual lesson.
days.hrs3: Full set. Ten-minute blank-page transformer. Off-by-one log.

days.week_title: Lists, binary search, and a transformer you can draw
days.coding: Redo the ugliest off-by-one from the log. Tighten stories 1–3 if they are still bullets.
days.second: Read the three stories aloud. Cut anything that is context without a decision.
days.drill: One redo or one story read-aloud.
days.hrs3: All three stories aloud. List binary-search variants you have not tried; do not solve them today.

weeks.title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
weeks.intent: Trees are the backbone of a huge share of coding rounds. Heaps handle top-k and scheduling. Tokenization explains bizarre model behavior, which interviewers on AI teams notice if you lack it.
weeks.exit: Traversals are muscle memory, BST validation is clean, and you can explain BPE at a whiteboard in two minutes.
weeks.dsa: Binary trees, BST, traversals, LCA, heaps, top-k.
weeks.systems: Recursion versus explicit stack. Heap as array.
weeks.ai: BPE, token weirdness, context measured in tokens not words.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 4: ambiguity. You started without a full spec.
weeks.rhythm: Tree drawings are mandatory. A heap day is not a tree day.
weeks.resources: NeetCode trees and heap. One good write-up of byte-pair encoding. Do not implement a full trainer.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: Inorder, preorder, postorder, level order. Recursive first, then one iterative with an explicit stack so you can talk about it.
days.problems: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal. Maximum Depth of Binary Tree. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal.
days.second: Tokenization: models do not see words. They see subword pieces. 'unhappiness' may be several tokens. Code and rare words cost more and sometimes split badly. Write five lines on BPE: merge frequent pairs until you hit a vocabulary size.
days.drill: Level order: name the queue invariant.
days.hrs3: All three traversals. Implement a toy BPE on a single repeated sentence so the merges are visible. Stop after it works once.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: Inorder is sorted. Validation must carry bounds, not just compare parent and child. Search and insert using the ordering.
days.problems: Validate Binary Search Tree. Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST. Kth Smallest Element in a BST.
days.second: Bring three real strings you have seen tokenize strangely (a number, a name, a URL). If you have a tokenizer tool or API, inspect them. If not, reason about which one is likely to split.
days.drill: Validate BST: explain why min/max bounds are required.
days.review: Patterns: BST bounds, not parent-only checks.
days.hrs3: Kth Smallest via inorder. Write the token notes.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: Pass the path down the recursion. Know when to backtrack the path list. Construction from preorder and inorder is the 'indexes, not slices' lesson.
days.problems: Path Sum. Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum as stretch. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder if Path Sum is clean.
days.second: Context budgeting: a 200k-token window is not 200k words. Estimate tokens as roughly three-quarters of a word in English, and say that this is a rough planning number, not a contract.
days.drill: Path Sum base cases: null versus leaf.
days.review: Patterns: DFS with accumulated state; backtrack.
days.hrs3: Maximum Path Sum only if you can state the 'gain from one child' idea first. Otherwise study a clean solution and retype it tomorrow.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: A heap is for repeated min or max, not for sorting everything. Know the language's heap (Python heapq is a min-heap). For top-k, a heap of size k beats a full sort when k is small, and you should say when it does not matter.
days.problems: Kth Largest Element in an Array. Last Stone Weight. Task Scheduler.
days.second: No new NLP. Add 'token ≠ word' and the rough English heuristic to the glossary.
days.drill: Say heap size and what the top represents.
days.review: Patterns: size-k heap; frequency then greedy slots for Task Scheduler.
days.min60: Kth Largest with a size-k heap.
days.hrs3: Task Scheduler. Explain the idle-slot formula if you use it, or the simulation if you simulate.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: Merge K sorted lists with a heap of current heads. Mention that the same idea is an external merge.
days.problems: Merge k Sorted Lists. Find Median from Data Stream as stretch.
days.second: Story seed 4: ambiguous requirements. What you assumed, how you checked, what you shipped.
days.drill: Merge k: state the heap key.
days.min60: Merge k Sorted Lists, or a clean study-and-retype if this is your first heap week and time is short.
days.hrs3: Median stream as stretch: two heaps, balance invariant written before code. Story seed drafted.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: Three timers. At least one BST and one traversal.
days.problems: Validate BST. Level order redo or LCA of a binary tree (not only BST). Kth Largest.
days.second: Retype the toy BPE or the token notes so they are in the repo.
days.drill: Validate BST timed.
days.hrs3: Full set plus two-minute spoken BPE.

days.week_title: Trees, heaps, and tokenization
days.coding: One blank-file tree redo. Read story seed 4 aloud and cut extra scene-setting.
days.second: List every tree pattern you can name without looking. Fill gaps tomorrow, do not cram tonight.
days.drill: Redo or the inventory, not both if energy is low.
days.hrs3: Inventory plus story. Schedule next week's graph drawings: grid, adjacency list.

weeks.title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
weeks.intent: Graph traversal is non-negotiable for SDE-2. The AI concept this week is how retrieval models differ: a bi-encoder embeds both sides separately; a cross-encoder scores a pair together and is used to rerank.
weeks.exit: BFS and DFS on grids and adjacency lists are clean, you can detect a cycle in a directed graph, and you can say when a reranker is worth the cost.
weeks.dsa: Graphs, BFS, DFS, topological sort, union-find.
weeks.systems: Adjacency list versus matrix. Visited-set bugs.
weeks.ai: Bi-encoder, cross-encoder, why rerank is a second stage.
weeks.behavior: Keep stories 1–4. No new seed unless one is missing.
weeks.rhythm: Draw the graph. Name visited handling before code.
weeks.resources: NeetCode graphs. A short note on dense retrieval versus cross-encoders from any serious RAG write-up.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Number of islands is the template: nested loops, skip visited, flood the component. Decide 4-direction versus 8-direction from the prompt.
days.problems: Number of Islands. Max Area of Island.
days.second: Write the retrieval two-stage: a fast bi-encoder narrows to top 50, a slower cross-encoder reranks the top 50. Cost is why you do not cross-encode the whole corpus.
days.drill: State visited update: mark when you enqueue, not when you dequeue, and say why.
days.min60: Number of Islands with the visited rule spoken.
days.hrs3: Max Area plus the two-stage paragraph. Clone Graph if islands felt easy.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Map old node to new node. DFS or BFS. The map is both the visited set and the result.
days.problems: Clone Graph. Pacific Atlantic Water Flow.
days.second: No new model. Draw bi-encoder (two towers, one dot product) versus cross-encoder (one scorer over the pair).
days.drill: Clone Graph: explain the map.
days.hrs3: Pacific Atlantic. Keep the drawing.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Kahn's algorithm: indegree, queue of zeros. A leftover node means a cycle. DFS postorder is the other version; know one cold and recognize the other.
days.second: Write when a reranker is wasted: tiny corpus, exact keyword task, or a latency budget that cannot take a second model. When it pays: top-k from embeddings is almost right but the order is wrong.
days.drill: Course Schedule: say how a cycle appears.
days.hrs3: Course Schedule II. Add the rerank decision to the AI notes.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Parent array, find with compression, union by rank or size. Count components. This is not the tool for shortest paths.
days.problems: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph. Redundant Connection.
days.second: One sentence you can say in a design interview: 'I will retrieve with a bi-encoder and rerank only the head of the list.'
days.drill: Implement find and union, then the problem.
days.hrs3: Redundant Connection. Practice the design sentence aloud.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Start the queue with every source. Distance is level. Word ladder is a graph even though it looks like strings; say how you build neighbors.
days.problems: Rotting Oranges. Word Ladder as stretch.
days.second: Story maintenance: read stories 1–4 and mark the one with the weakest result. You will need a number, a user effect, or a clear before/after.
days.drill: Rotting Oranges: why multi-source, not a loop of BFS.
days.hrs3: Word Ladder neighbor-generation plan, even if the code is not finished. Strengthen the weakest story's result line.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Three timers. One grid, one topo or union-find, one redo.
days.problems: Number of Islands. Course Schedule. Clone Graph or Rotting Oranges.
days.second: No new AI reading. Speak the two-stage retrieval sentence once.
days.drill: One graph, visited rule spoken.
days.review: Log the bug if you marked visited too late.
days.hrs3: Full set plus the spoken sentence recorded in notes as a line you will reuse in Week 12.

days.week_title: Graphs, and bi-encoders versus cross-encoders
days.coding: Redo one graph from a blank file. Update the weakest story result.
days.second: List graph templates you own: flood, clone, topo, DSU, multi-source. Star the shaky one for a 30-minute slot next week.
days.drill: Redo the shaky template only.
days.hrs3: Template list and story result line.

weeks.title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
weeks.intent: DP is where candidates stall. This week is one-dimensional patterns only, plus the vocabulary of approximate nearest neighbor search so vector databases are not magic later.
weeks.exit: You can write a recurrence before code for house robber, coin change, and a knapsack-style decision. You can define HNSW and IVF as index families, not products.
weeks.dsa: 1D DP, knapsack, coin change, decision DP. Light graph leftovers.
weeks.systems: Time and space of the DP table. Rolling arrays as a follow-up.
weeks.ai: ANN, HNSW, IVF, recall versus latency.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 5: raising the bar or reviewing someone else's design.
weeks.rhythm: Recurrence in a comment before code. If you cannot write it, you are not ready to type.
weeks.resources: NeetCode 1D DP. One vendor or textbook page on HNSW. Do not tune index parameters yet.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: State: dp[i] is the best answer using the first i items or reaching i. Transition in a comment. Base cases explicit.
days.second: Brute nearest neighbor is a scan of every vector. Approximate indexes skip most of them. HNSW is a layered small-world graph. IVF clusters vectors and searches only some clusters. Both can miss true neighbors. That miss rate is recall of the index, which is not the same phrase as retrieval recall, but you should not confuse the two.
days.concept: ANN is allowed to be wrong a little
days.drill: House Robber recurrence spoken.
days.review: Patterns: dp[i] from dp[i-1] and dp[i-2].
days.min60: House Robber with the recurrence comment.
days.hrs3: House Robber II (circular) only after the linear version is clean. Write the HNSW/IVF definitions in your words.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: Coins can be reused. Decide loop order and be able to say whether order matters for combinations versus permutations.
days.problems: Coin Change. Coin Change II if the first is clean.
days.second: Write a tradeoff: higher index recall costs latency and memory. For a 2 million document help center, say you would measure recall@10 of the index on a golden neighbor set before trusting a diagram.
days.drill: Coin Change: what does dp[a] mean?
days.hrs3: Coin Change II. Add the tradeoff note.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: Each item once. Classic knapsack shape even if the problem is worded as a partition or a target sum.
days.problems: Partition Equal Subset Sum. Target Sum as stretch.
days.second: Name three vector databases you might mention and one reason each exists: pgvector when Postgres is already the system of record, a dedicated engine when you need filtering and scale, a local library like FAISS when the corpus fits in a service. Do not memorize marketing.
days.drill: State include/exclude.
days.hrs3: Target Sum. The three-home note for indexes.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: dp[i] means the prefix of length i is solvable. Check dictionary words ending at i, or single-token decisions.
days.second: No new index theory. Draw ingest versus query: ingest embeds and upserts; query embeds the question and searches. Filters (tenant, language, date) should use metadata, not a prompt.
days.drill: Decode Ways: the two-digit branch.
days.hrs3: Word Break. Draw the ingest/query split.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: O(n^2) DP first and say it. The patience-sorting O(n log n) method is a follow-up, not the first version you code under stress.
days.second: Story seed 5: a review or a quality bar. What was weak, what you asked for, what changed. SDE-2 signal is that you improve work you do not personally own.
days.drill: LIS: define dp[i] as the longest subsequence ending at i.
days.hrs3: Study the n log n idea only as reading. Draft story seed 5.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: Three timers. Recurrence comment required even under the timer. If the comment is empty, the solution does not count as clean.
days.problems: House Robber. Coin Change. Decode Ways or Partition.
days.second: Speak the ANN one-liner: approximate search trades a little recall for a lot of latency.
days.drill: One DP with a written recurrence.
days.review: Log problems where you coded before the recurrence.
days.hrs3: Full set. ANN one-liner in the notes.

days.week_title: Dynamic programming starts, indexes get named
days.coding: Retype one DP from memory. Read story 5 aloud.
days.second: Make a DP state cheat: one line per problem you did, 'dp[i] means'. This page is worth more than a new problem.
days.drill: The state cheat sheet for this week's problems.
days.hrs3: Retype plus story plus cheat sheet.

weeks.title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
weeks.intent: Two-dimensional DP and the chunking decisions that decide whether RAG works. This is the week coding and AI start to feel like one job.
weeks.exit: You can set up a 2D table for unique paths, LCS, and edit distance. You can choose a chunk size with a reason and name three chunking failure modes.
weeks.dsa: Grid DP, LCS, edit distance, interval intro only if 2D is stable.
weeks.systems: Space optimization as a follow-up sentence.
weeks.ai: Chunk size, overlap, structure-aware splits, metadata.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 6: a miss or a failed launch. Own your part.
weeks.rhythm: Draw the table. Fill one row by hand before coding.
weeks.resources: NeetCode 2D DP. A serious RAG chunking article. Keep a sample PDF or markdown note you will chunk in Week 13.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: Unique paths: dp[r][c] from top and left. Obstacles zero a cell. Paint the first row and column carefully.
days.second: Chunking: fixed tokens with overlap is the baseline, not the ideal. Splitting on headings, functions, or speaker turns keeps ideas intact. A chunk that starts mid-sentence retrieves badly. Write your default: split on structure first, then fall back to tokens, with overlap only when sentences cross the cut.
days.drill: Fill a 3x3 unique-paths table by hand.
days.review: Patterns: grid sum from top and left.
days.hrs3: Unique Paths II. Write the chunking default in the AI notes.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: dp[i][j] is LCS of the prefixes. Match diagonal, else max of dropping one side. This pattern reappears in edit distance.
days.second: Failure modes: chunks too big (the answer is diluted), too small (the fact is split from its condition), no metadata (you retrieve another tenant's policy), overlap used as a substitute for bad boundaries.
days.drill: LCS: say the diagonal case.
days.hrs3: Write the four failure modes with a one-line example each, using a fake employee-handbook policy.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: Insert, delete, replace. Base row and column are the costs of turning a string into empty. This is a common hard-medium; the table is the whole trick.
days.second: Metadata you almost always want: source, title, section, updated_at, tenant or visibility, language. The model should not be the one enforcing access control.
days.concept: Access control is not a prompt
days.drill: Edit distance base row spoken.
days.hrs3: A second pass on edit distance from a blank file tomorrow is better than a new problem today if this was shaky. Write the metadata list.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: If edit distance was clean, do one more 2D. If it was not, redo edit distance from blank and skip the new problem. That choice is the point of this day.
days.problems: Longest Palindromic Subsequence, only if edit distance was clean. Otherwise a blank redo.
days.second: Parent and child chunks, conceptual: retrieve a small precise chunk, then expand to the parent section for the model. You will implement a simple version in the RAG project.
days.drill: Make the redo-versus-new decision explicitly and write it in the log.
days.min60: The redo or the new problem, not a third thing.
days.hrs3: Both, only if the first was finished inside 40 minutes. Parent-chunk note.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: Sort by end time to count the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. Sort by start to merge. These are greedy, and you should not force a DP table.
days.second: Story seed 6: a failure. What you missed, how you found out, what you changed in the system or the process. No vague 'we learned a lot'.
days.drill: Say which end you sort on, and why.
days.review: Patterns: sort by end; sort by start and merge.
days.hrs3: Non-overlapping Intervals. Story seed 6.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: 45 minutes, one medium, out loud, no notes. Then 15 minutes of what an interviewer would have written: clarity, correctness, pace, tests. This is a mock, not a shame session.
days.problems: Pick a medium you have not memorized from DP or graphs.
days.second: No AI study during the mock. After the retro, one paragraph: would you pass an L4 coding round today? Yes, borderline, or no, plus the single biggest gap.
days.drill: The 45-minute mock. Retro can be five lines.
days.hrs3: Mock, retro, and a 20-minute untimed repair of the biggest gap. Do not start a second problem.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: Retype the mock problem cleanly if it was messy. Update the DP state cheat with this week's tables.
days.second: Read story 6. If the 'change' line is missing, it is not an SDE-2 story yet.
days.drill: State cheat update.
days.hrs3: Redo plus story plus a one-line plan for Week 8 mocks.

weeks.title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
weeks.intent: Close the coding-pattern tour: backtracking, greedy leftovers, tries, light bit operations. Pair it with hybrid search, because semantic-only retrieval fails keyword-exact tasks like error codes and SKUs.
weeks.exit: You have a repeatable backtracking template, a trie you can code, and a spoken answer for when to combine BM25 with vectors.
weeks.dsa: Backtracking, subsets, permutations, tries, bits, greedy check.
weeks.systems: OOP design one session, because some loops still ask it.
weeks.ai: BM25, hybrid fusion, exact filters versus semantic rank.
weeks.rhythm: Template first for backtracking. One mock on Saturday.
weeks.resources: NeetCode backtracking and trie. Any clear note on BM25 and reciprocal rank fusion. You do not need the full BM25 derivation.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Choose, explore, unchoose. Start index to avoid duplicates. Draw the decision tree for a three-element set.
days.second: BM25 is lexical: rare terms that match exactly matter more. Embeddings miss exact IDs and can be distracted by paraphrases. Hybrid means you run both and merge. A simple interview answer is: normalize scores or use reciprocal rank fusion, then keep the union of the two lists.
days.drill: Draw the subsets tree, then code.
days.hrs3: Combination Sum. Write the hybrid answer in four sentences.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: A used array, or swapping. Word search is a grid DFS with a visited cell and a backtrack.
days.second: Exact metadata filters are not the same as hybrid rank. Tenant, type, and date are filters. Wording is rank. Say this distinction out loud; mixing them is a common design-round mistake.
days.drill: Word Search: when do you mark visited?
days.hrs3: Word Search. Filter-versus-rank note.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Insert and search character by character. Word versus prefix. This structure is also how you talk about autocomplete later.
days.problems: Implement Trie. Design Add and Search Words Data Structure if the first is clean.
days.second: A worked example on paper: query 'ERR_5042 timeout'. BM25 hits the code. Embeddings hit a paragraph about timeouts that never mentions the code. Hybrid returns both. The model should prefer the chunk that contains the code.
days.drill: Trie node: map of children plus end flag.
days.hrs3: Wildcard search as stretch. Keep the error-code example in the systems folder; you will reuse it.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: You need XOR for 'single number', a left shift as multiply-by-two awareness, and the courage to say when bits are a micro-optimization the interviewer did not ask for.
days.problems: Single Number. Number of 1 Bits. Counting Bits if those are easy.
days.second: No new retrieval theory. Add hybrid search to the glossary with the error-code example.
days.drill: Single Number: why XOR cancels pairs.
days.min60: Single Number plus the spoken XOR.
days.hrs3: Counting Bits. Glossary update.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Design a parking lot or a deck of cards. Clarify, name entities, relationships, and one extension. This is not leetcode. Some companies, and some Google RRK conversations, still wander here. Spend one hour, not a week.
days.problems: Parking lot: levels, spots, vehicle types, one tick of parking and leaving.
days.second: Story seed 7: cross-team. What you needed, how you asked, what changed for the user. SDE-2 scope often shows up here rather than in a solo algorithm.
days.drill: Parking lot entities on paper. Code only the types if time remains.
days.review: File it under stories/systems, not under DSA patterns.
days.hrs3: A short code skeleton and story seed 7.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: 45 minutes out loud. Pick from backtracking, trie, or a graph so you are not only mocking DP. Retro in the same format as Week 7.
days.second: Compare this retro to Week 7. One sentence: what improved, what did not.
days.drill: Mock only.
days.hrs3: Mock, retro, comparison sentence, 20-minute repair.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Build a one-page pattern index: for each pattern, one trigger phrase ('sorted and pair' → two pointers) and one problem name. This page is your warm-up for the rest of the plan.
days.second: Read stories 5–7. You should now have seven seeds. They can be ugly. They cannot be empty.
days.drill: Start the pattern index with ten lines.
days.hrs3: Full index across Weeks 1–8 and a story gap check.

weeks.title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
weeks.intent: SDE-2 design and debugging rounds assume operating systems, networking, and databases. This week is interview depth, not a degree. Keep a light coding maintenance habit so patterns do not rot.
weeks.exit: You can explain an index, a transaction, HTTP versus a connection, and a lock. You can write a SQL query with a join and a window or a group-by without a search tab.
weeks.dsa: Maintenance only: four problems across the week, from the pattern index.
weeks.systems: OS, networking, SQL, indexes, transactions, caching.
weeks.ai: Read a plain-language summary of the original RAG paper so Week 13 is implementation, not first contact.
weeks.rhythm: 60 minutes of CS, 30 minutes of coding maintenance, notes in complete sentences.
weeks.resources: Selected chapters of Designing Data-Intensive Applications for storage and replication ideas, in interview language. Use The Missing Semester or your own OS/networking notes if you already have a course background. SQLBolt or a local Postgres for the SQL day. Lewis et al. RAG paper abstract plus a good blog recap.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance problem, 30 minutes: one tree or graph from the index.
days.problems: One redo from the pattern index, timed 30 minutes.
days.second: Interview answers you need: process versus thread, race, deadlock (the four conditions by name is enough), mutex versus semaphore at a sentence each, why a CPU-bound pool sized past the core count does not help. Skip kernel trivia.
days.drill: Explain deadlock with a two-lock example.
days.review: CS notes: one page, processes and locks.
days.min60: The spoken deadlock example plus one maintenance problem.
days.hrs3: Write a tiny threaded counter in your language that races, then fix it with a lock. Do not build a thread-pool framework.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one binary search variant, 30 minutes.
days.second: Learn the interview latency table as orders of magnitude, and label it as an approximation: L1 nanoseconds, RAM ~100 ns, SSD read much larger, same-datacenter round trip under a millisecond to a few milliseconds, cross-continent tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Use it to reject designs, not to pretend precision.
days.drill: Estimate: is 200 ms reasonable for a disk-backed query that crosses regions? Say why or why not.
days.hrs3: Add cache, RAM, and network rows with a sentence on what design move each number forbids.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one sliding window, 30 minutes.
days.second: What you must be able to draw: DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS, HTTP request, status codes you will actually mention (200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 500). REST versus RPC in one sentence. gRPC when you want typed internal calls. Timeouts, retries, and idempotency as the safety story for retries.
days.drill: Explain why a retried POST can double-charge unless you have an idempotency key.
days.review: Networking page in the CS notes.
days.min60: Status codes plus the idempotency sentence.
days.hrs3: Draw the full request path from browser to app server. Add timeouts to the drawing.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one DP with a recurrence comment, 30 minutes.
days.second: Create a tiny orders and users example. Write: join, filter, group by with having, and one window function (row_number or sum over partition). Explain an index as a structure that speeds reads and costs writes. Composite index column order matters.
days.drill: Write the join without looking.
days.hrs3: Window function plus a paragraph on when an index is useless (leading-column mismatch, function wrapped on the column).

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one heap or interval problem, 25 minutes.
days.second: ACID in your own words. Isolation anomalies you can name: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, and the practical punchline that 'serializable is safer and often slower'. Mention row locks versus optimistic version columns. You are not implementing a database.
days.drill: Give one example of a lost update on a balance.
days.hrs3: Read a DDIA passage on replication lag and write five lines on read-your-writes.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: No coding maintenance today. Use the time on systems.
days.second: Cache aside versus write-through, named only. TTL, stampede, and the question 'what is the source of truth?'. Then read a RAG paper summary: retrieve documents, stuff them into the prompt, generate. Write three weaknesses the original setup has, using what you already know about chunks and hybrid search.
days.drill: Define cache aside.
days.hrs3: Full caching page and three weaknesses tied to chunks, citations, and evals.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Explain, out loud, without notes: index, transaction, retry with idempotency, lock. Then one coding redo.
days.second: Story seed 8: user-visible impact. Who had a better day because of the change, and how you know.
days.drill: Two of the four spoken explanations.
days.review: Record gaps in the CS page headings.
days.hrs3: All four explanations, one redo, story seed 8.

weeks.title: A design method, then three small systems
weeks.intent: SDE-2 design is a method plus a few classics. You are designing one service well, not the internet. Numbers are estimates you can revise when the interviewer changes a constraint.
weeks.exit: You can run the same agenda on three different products: requirements, estimates, API, data model, happy path, bottleneck, tradeoff.
weeks.dsa: Two maintenance problems this week, not every day.
weeks.systems: URL shortener, rate limiter, a small paste or file service.
weeks.ai: On paper only: where semantic search would sit inside one of these designs. Do not build it.
weeks.behavior: Tell stories 1 and 6 aloud against a timer.
weeks.rhythm: 40 minutes design on paper or a tablet, 10 minutes retro against the agenda. Resist tool-collecting.
weeks.resources: ByteByteGo or a Grokking-style walkthrough for the classics, then close the book and redo from blank. The method matters more than their boxes.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: One maintenance medium, 30 minutes, from a weak pattern.
days.second: Write your agenda on a card: (1) clarify functional requirements and non-goals, (2) scale sketch, (3) API, (4) data model, (5) high-level path, (6) the bottleneck you will actually go deep on, (7) tradeoffs and failure. Practice it on 'design a URL shortener' for 35 minutes without looking at a solution.
days.drill: Run steps 1–4 only, out loud.
days.hrs3: Full 35-minute pass plus a written scale sketch: reads per second, writes per second, storage for five years. Label every number as an assumption.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: No new coding pattern.
days.second: Blank redo of the shortener. Go deep on key generation (random versus counter), redirect latency, and cache. Mention analytics as a non-goal unless asked. Say what you would shard if writes grew.
days.drill: Draw only the read path.
days.review: systems/url-shortener.md with assumptions at the top.
days.hrs3: Full redo and a paragraph on how you would add 'similar URL' semantic lookup without putting a model on the redirect path.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: One maintenance problem, 25 minutes.
days.second: Token bucket versus sliding window, in words and a sketch. Where it runs: API gateway, per user and per IP. What you store. How clocks and multiple limiter nodes drift. Return 429. This design is also how you protect an LLM endpoint from a runaway client.
days.drill: Speak token bucket refill.
days.hrs3: Add a second key: limit by user and a stricter global limit for an expensive model route.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: None.
days.second: Design a paste service. Metadata in a database, body in object storage once past a size threshold, cache hot pastes, expiry. Mention virus scanning only if you have time. The point is separating metadata from blobs.
days.drill: Name the source of truth for the paste body.
days.hrs3: Add CDN for reads and a note on cache invalidation when a paste is deleted.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Build a small estimation card: seconds in a day, QPS from daily active users and actions, storage as rows times bytes times replication. Practice one estimate, then change a constraint when an imaginary interviewer says 'make it 10x' and show what breaks first.
days.drill: One QPS estimate on paper.
days.hrs3: The 10x follow-up on the paste service.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: None during the mock.
days.second: 40 minutes: design a rate limiter or the shortener, out loud, agenda card only. Retro: did you skip requirements, did you invent numbers, did you go deep on one bottleneck or draw fifteen boxes?
days.drill: Mock. Five-line retro.
days.hrs3: Mock, retro, and a 15-minute redraw of the weakest section.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: No coding.
days.second: Tell story 1 and story 6 in two minutes each. Record yourself or sit with a friend. Cut the preamble. End on the result.
days.drill: One story, two minutes.
days.review: Note the sentences you will delete.
days.hrs3: Both stories plus a rewritten opening line for each.

weeks.title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
weeks.intent: The second design week is fan-out, messaging, and failure. These are the diagrams L4 interviewers use to see whether you have operated anything real.
weeks.exit: You can compare fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read, design a chat inbox, and explain at-least-once delivery plus idempotency.
weeks.systems: News feed, chat, notifications, queues, consistency menu.
weeks.ai: Design the ingestion path for a support-doc bot on paper. Still no framework.
weeks.behavior: Stories 2 and 3 under a two-minute timer.
weeks.rhythm: One system a day. Reuse the same agenda card.
weeks.resources: Classic feed and chat write-ups, then blank redos. A chapter or essay on delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once as a careful claim.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: One maintenance medium.
days.second: Design a simplified home feed. Celebrity problem: fan-out-on-write is painful for a user with millions of followers, so mix strategies. Ranking can be a later section; do not open with machine learning. Storage for posts versus storage for timelines.
days.drill: Define fan-out-on-write in two sentences.
days.hrs3: Add a sentence on where a ranking model would sit, and what happens when it times out: show a chronological fallback.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: 1:1 chat. Message table, inbox per user, online delivery via a connection, offline via stored messages. Read receipts as optional. Ordering per conversation. Media goes to blob storage. Presence is a separate small path.
days.drill: Draw the send path for one message.
days.hrs3: Group chat fan-out and a note on why 'exactly once' display is usually idempotent message ids.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Design notifications: event in, preference check, fan out to email, push, and in-app. Retries, dead letter, user-level rate limits so you do not mail someone fifty times. This is a queue problem wearing a product costume.
days.drill: Name the queue and the idempotency key.
days.hrs3: Add a digest mode: collapse bursts into one message.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: Build a one-page menu you can pull out in any design: leader/follower replication, async lag, quorums in words, conflict on a counter versus a document, outbox pattern so you do not dual-write to a database and a queue by hope. Pick the feed and say what can be stale.
days.drill: Explain read-your-writes for the person who just posted.
days.min60: The outbox idea in five sentences.
days.hrs3: Apply the menu to chat message send: what must be durable before you ack the sender.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: Design ingestion for a help-center bot: crawl, parse, chunk, embed, upsert with metadata, delete when a doc is unpublished. Query path: auth, embed question, filter by product and visibility, retrieve, optional rerank, prompt with citations, abstain if nothing clears a threshold. You are not choosing a vendor logo. You are naming responsibilities.
days.drill: Draw ingest only.
days.hrs3: Full query path and a failure: the doc changed and the index is stale. How does the user see freshness?

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: 40 minutes: chat or notifications, agenda card, out loud. Retro aimed at one question: did failure and retries show up before the interviewer asked?
days.drill: Mock.
days.hrs3: Mock and a redraw of the failure path.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: No coding.
days.second: Two-minute tellings. Story 2 is the incident. Story 3 is the disagreement. Check that story 3 does not insult the other person.
days.drill: One story.
days.hrs3: Both, plus a note on which leadership theme each one proves.

weeks.title: Embeddings you can measure
weeks.intent: Stop reading and build. A small similarity search over a corpus you control, with an eval of ten questions. This is the project you can talk about in an AI-leaning SDE-2 loop.
weeks.exit: A script embeds a corpus, stores vectors, answers ten questions by nearest neighbor, and you have a written score of how many neighbors were actually relevant.
weeks.dsa: Three maintenance problems across the week.
weeks.systems: You are designing the smallest vertical slice of semantic search.
weeks.ai: Embeddings, a local or hosted index, recall on a tiny golden set.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 9: something you improved that was not assigned.
weeks.rhythm: Build in small commits. If an API key is missing, use a local model or even a deterministic bag-of-words fallback and document the gap. Do not stop the week for credentials.
weeks.resources: sentence-transformers or any embedding API. FAISS, Chroma, or even a NumPy scan if the corpus is tiny. The point is the eval, not the vendor.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One maintenance problem so coding does not go cold.
days.problems: One medium from the pattern index.
days.second: Pick a corpus you may store: your own notes, a public-domain handbook, or twenty pages you write about a fake product. Write ten questions whose answers live in that corpus, and record the passage that should be retrieved. This golden set is the project. The model is not.
days.drill: Write five questions and their source passages.
days.hrs3: Ten questions. At least two should be traps: the words match the wrong section.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: None.
days.second: Chunk the corpus with the rule from Week 7. Embed chunks. For each question, embed it and rank chunks by cosine. Print the top three. Use a brute-force scan if the corpus is small, and say that a real index replaces the scan.
days.drill: One question, top three printed.
days.review: Commit the script and a sample run.
days.hrs3: All ten questions printed. Note which trap questions failed.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Score hit@3: was the labeled passage in the top three? Write the misses in a table with a suspected reason: bad chunk boundary, synonym, too-broad chunk, or tie. Do not 'fix' by changing the label to match the model.
days.drill: Score five questions.
days.min60: A written hit@3 on five questions.
days.hrs3: All ten, plus a one-line fix you will try tomorrow (overlap, heading-based split, or a metadata field).

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: None.
days.second: Apply exactly one retrieval change. Re-run the same ten questions. Report the new hit@3 next to the old one. If it got worse, keep the note; negative results are interview gold.
days.drill: Ship the one change.
days.min60: The change and a partial rescore.
days.hrs3: Full rescore and a paragraph a hiring manager could read.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Add a metadata field such as product or visibility. Show a query that must not return a chunk from the wrong product even if the vector is close. This is the access-control lesson from Week 7, in code.
days.drill: One filtered query.
days.review: Document the filter in the README.
days.hrs3: A test that fails if the wrong product appears in the top three.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: No new features.
days.second: Five-minute spoken walkthrough: corpus, chunking, embedding, ranking, metric, the change you tried, what you would do at a million documents (ANN index, reranker, hybrid for error codes). Record it.
days.drill: Speak it once, messy.
days.hrs3: A clean take and a diagram.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One timed medium, 35 minutes.
days.second: Story seed 9: an improvement nobody assigned. Initiative without chaos. What you noticed, what you changed, how you checked it was better.
days.drill: The story seed in four lines.
days.hrs3: Story plus the timed medium.

weeks.title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
weeks.intent: Generation is the easy demo and the hard product. This week adds a prompt, citations, a refusal path, and twenty questions. Frameworks are optional; a raw API call is a valid implementation.
weeks.exit: Given a question, the system either answers with a citation to a retrieved chunk or says it does not know. You have a written score on twenty questions.
weeks.systems: The support-bot sketch from Week 11, now a small running slice.
weeks.ai: RAG, grounding, abstain, basic hallucination checks.
weeks.behavior: Story 8 and 9 told in two minutes.
weeks.rhythm: Extend last week's project. Do not start over in a new repo unless the old one is a dead end.
weeks.resources: The model API you already picked. A prompt file in git. DeepLearning.AI's RAG and eval material if you want a second explanation after you have built yours.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Take the top chunks and a question. Prompt the model to answer only from those chunks and to quote the chunk id it used. If the chunks are irrelevant, it must say it does not know. Save the prompt in git.
days.drill: One question end to end with a citation.
days.hrs3: Five questions. Mark any answer that used knowledge not in the chunks.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: None.
days.second: Add five questions whose answers are not in the corpus. A correct system refuses. A system that invents a confident answer fails, even if the prose is lovely. Tune the prompt or a similarity threshold until at least some of these refuse. Record what you changed.
days.drill: One out-of-corpus question refuses.
days.hrs3: Five out-of-corpus questions scored.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Expand to twenty questions: some factual, some that need two chunks, some traps, some out of corpus. Score faithfulness (did it stick to the text) separately from retrieval hit. A retrieved right passage with a wrong summary is a generation miss, not a vector miss.
days.drill: Score five more questions in the two-column way.
days.hrs3: All twenty scored in two columns.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: None.
days.second: Return the passage text, not only an id. If you cannot highlight the supporting sentence, do not claim a citation. Fix one unfaithful answer by changing the prompt or the context, then rescore only the affected rows.
days.drill: One answer with the passage attached.
days.hrs3: Rescore the unfaithful rows and write whether the fix was prompt, chunk, or retrieval.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.theme: Hybrid or rerank, one of them
days.coding: None.
days.second: If your misses are exact codes or names, add a simple lexical overlap score and merge it with cosine. If your misses are 'right documents, wrong order', add a rerank step even if the reranker is just a cross-encoder you call on five chunks, or a model asked to pick the best chunk. One of these, not a platform rewrite.
days.drill: Implement the merge or the rerank on a single query.
days.hrs3: Rescore the miss list only, and keep the change if the score improved.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: No features.
days.second: Eight-minute talk: retrieval metric, generation metric, refusal, the change that helped, what you would not trust this demo to do in production (privacy, freshness, adversarial users). Production honesty is an SDE-2 signal.
days.drill: Speak the 'would not ship' paragraph.
days.hrs3: Full eight minutes, recorded.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: Fix one real bug in the RAG script. That counts as engineering practice.
days.problems: None from LeetCode unless the script is already solid.
days.second: Tell stories 8 and 9 in two minutes. Map each to a company theme you care about: Google's collaboration and ambiguity, Amazon's ownership and customer obsession, Meta's impact and move-fast-with-stability.
days.drill: One story mapped to one theme.
days.review: A theme tag on each story.
days.hrs3: Both stories and the bug fix committed.

weeks.title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
weeks.intent: Frameworks are interview vocabulary and sometimes the fastest way to a prototype. They are not the design. You should be able to build the same tool-using flow with and without a framework, and you should know what state LangGraph is holding.
weeks.exit: A small graph: retrieve, decide, call a tool, answer. You can draw the state and the edges. You can say when a raw SDK is the better choice.
weeks.dsa: Two maintenance problems, ideally under a 35-minute timer.
weeks.systems: Tool calling is an API design problem.
weeks.ai: Function calling, LangChain LCEL at a skim, LangGraph state and checkpoints.
weeks.behavior: Story seed 10: a conflict between speed and quality.
weeks.rhythm: Read docs only to unblock the day's slice. No framework tourism.
weeks.resources: Current LangChain and LangGraph docs for the exact APIs, which change. Your model provider's tool-calling guide. If versions fight you for more than 45 minutes, write the graph as plain Python functions and document that choice.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: One timed medium.
days.second: Define one tool, for example a fake order-status function that reads a local dict. Send the tool schema to the model, execute the call yourself, send the result back, and get a final answer. Log every message. You own the loop.
days.drill: One tool round-trip logged.
days.hrs3: A second tool, plus a test where the model should not call a tool (a chit-chat question).

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: None.
days.second: Rebuild only the retrieval chain in LangChain or LCEL: loader or your chunks, retriever, prompt, model. Then write a note: what it shortened, what it hid, and one place you would drop it (tight latency, simple script, confusing stack traces during an incident). Knowing when not to use it is the SDE-2 answer.
days.drill: The chain runs one question.
days.review: The judgment note in the README.
days.min60: Chain plus the start of the note.
days.hrs3: Chain, note, and a comparison of logs versus your raw script.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: One timed medium from a different pattern than yesterday.
days.second: Model the bot as a graph. State: question, documents, tool result, draft, citations. Nodes: retrieve, grade or abstain, tool, answer. Edges: if documents are weak, abstain; if the question needs order status, call the tool; else answer from docs. Checkpointing means you can resume; say that, and turn it on only if the API is painless.
days.drill: Draw the graph on paper before installing anything.
days.hrs3: The graph handles answer, abstain, and one tool.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: None.
days.second: Add one interrupt: if the tool would 'refund' or otherwise mutate state, stop and require an explicit yes in the terminal. Even a fake refund teaches the production idea. Multi-agent swarms are out of scope; write one sentence on why a single graph with tools is your default.
days.drill: The interrupt triggers once.
days.hrs3: Interrupt plus the anti-swarm sentence.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: None.
days.second: Read what the Model Context Protocol is: a standard way for a host to give a model tools and data sources. You do not need to write a server unless you want a stretch. You do need to say how it differs from a one-off function call: discovery and reuse across hosts. Note the trust issue: a tool is code execution with extra steps, so you treat tool descriptions as untrusted input.
days.drill: Write the definition in five lines.
days.hrs3: Definition plus a threat you would actually mitigate: a tool that returns text telling the model to ignore the policy. Your mitigation is to keep system instructions and tool output in separate roles and to validate tool arguments. Do not build an attack.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: No new nodes.
days.second: Ten-minute explanation to an imaginary interviewer: why a graph, what the state holds, where you abstain, where a human confirms, what you would trace in production. If you skipped LangGraph for plain Python, explain that decision with the same confidence.
days.drill: Five minutes, notes allowed.
days.hrs3: Ten minutes without the drawing in hand, then look down and see what you forgot.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: One coding redo, 30 minutes.
days.second: Story seed 10: you were pushed to ship and you saw a quality risk. What you negotiated, what you cut on purpose, what you refused to cut.
days.drill: Four-line seed.
days.hrs3: Seed expanded and the coding redo.

weeks.title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
weeks.intent: The last teaching week. Cost, latency, evals, privacy, and the ways Google, Amazon, Meta, and AI teams weigh the same skills differently. After this, you are in mock-and-apply mode.
