days.drill: The 45-minute mock. Retro can be five lines.
days.hrs3: Mock, retro, and a 20-minute untimed repair of the biggest gap. Do not start a second problem.

days.week_title: Grids, edit distance, and how chunks go wrong
days.coding: Retype the mock problem cleanly if it was messy. Update the DP state cheat with this week's tables.
days.second: Read story 6. If the 'change' line is missing, it is not an SDE-2 story yet.
days.drill: State cheat update.
days.hrs3: Redo plus story plus a one-line plan for Week 8 mocks.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Choose, explore, unchoose. Start index to avoid duplicates. Draw the decision tree for a three-element set.
days.second: BM25 is lexical: rare terms that match exactly matter more. Embeddings miss exact IDs and can be distracted by paraphrases. Hybrid means you run both and merge. A simple interview answer is: normalize scores or use reciprocal rank fusion, then keep the union of the two lists.
days.drill: Draw the subsets tree, then code.
days.hrs3: Combination Sum. Write the hybrid answer in four sentences.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: A used array, or swapping. Word search is a grid DFS with a visited cell and a backtrack.
days.second: Exact metadata filters are not the same as hybrid rank. Tenant, type, and date are filters. Wording is rank. Say this distinction out loud; mixing them is a common design-round mistake.
days.drill: Word Search: when do you mark visited?
days.hrs3: Word Search. Filter-versus-rank note.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Insert and search character by character. Word versus prefix. This structure is also how you talk about autocomplete later.
days.problems: Implement Trie. Design Add and Search Words Data Structure if the first is clean.
days.second: A worked example on paper: query 'ERR_5042 timeout'. BM25 hits the code. Embeddings hit a paragraph about timeouts that never mentions the code. Hybrid returns both. The model should prefer the chunk that contains the code.
days.drill: Trie node: map of children plus end flag.
days.hrs3: Wildcard search as stretch. Keep the error-code example in the systems folder; you will reuse it.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: You need XOR for 'single number', a left shift as multiply-by-two awareness, and the courage to say when bits are a micro-optimization the interviewer did not ask for.
days.problems: Single Number. Number of 1 Bits. Counting Bits if those are easy.
days.second: No new retrieval theory. Add hybrid search to the glossary with the error-code example.
days.drill: Single Number: why XOR cancels pairs.
days.min60: Single Number plus the spoken XOR.
days.hrs3: Counting Bits. Glossary update.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Design a parking lot or a deck of cards. Clarify, name entities, relationships, and one extension. This is not leetcode. Some companies, and some Google RRK conversations, still wander here. Spend one hour, not a week.
days.problems: Parking lot: levels, spots, vehicle types, one tick of parking and leaving.
days.second: Story seed 7: cross-team. What you needed, how you asked, what changed for the user. SDE-2 scope often shows up here rather than in a solo algorithm.
days.drill: Parking lot entities on paper. Code only the types if time remains.
days.review: File it under stories/systems, not under DSA patterns.
days.hrs3: A short code skeleton and story seed 7.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: 45 minutes out loud. Pick from backtracking, trie, or a graph so you are not only mocking DP. Retro in the same format as Week 7.
days.second: Compare this retro to Week 7. One sentence: what improved, what did not.
days.drill: Mock only.
days.hrs3: Mock, retro, comparison sentence, 20-minute repair.

days.week_title: Search, tries, and hybrid retrieval
days.coding: Build a one-page pattern index: for each pattern, one trigger phrase ('sorted and pair' → two pointers) and one problem name. This page is your warm-up for the rest of the plan.
days.second: Read stories 5–7. You should now have seven seeds. They can be ugly. They cannot be empty.
days.drill: Start the pattern index with ten lines.
days.hrs3: Full index across Weeks 1–8 and a story gap check.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance problem, 30 minutes: one tree or graph from the index.
days.problems: One redo from the pattern index, timed 30 minutes.
days.second: Interview answers you need: process versus thread, race, deadlock (the four conditions by name is enough), mutex versus semaphore at a sentence each, why a CPU-bound pool sized past the core count does not help. Skip kernel trivia.
days.drill: Explain deadlock with a two-lock example.
days.review: CS notes: one page, processes and locks.
days.min60: The spoken deadlock example plus one maintenance problem.
days.hrs3: Write a tiny threaded counter in your language that races, then fix it with a lock. Do not build a thread-pool framework.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one binary search variant, 30 minutes.
days.second: Learn the interview latency table as orders of magnitude, and label it as an approximation: L1 nanoseconds, RAM ~100 ns, SSD read much larger, same-datacenter round trip under a millisecond to a few milliseconds, cross-continent tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Use it to reject designs, not to pretend precision.
days.drill: Estimate: is 200 ms reasonable for a disk-backed query that crosses regions? Say why or why not.
days.hrs3: Add cache, RAM, and network rows with a sentence on what design move each number forbids.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one sliding window, 30 minutes.
days.second: What you must be able to draw: DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS, HTTP request, status codes you will actually mention (200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 500). REST versus RPC in one sentence. gRPC when you want typed internal calls. Timeouts, retries, and idempotency as the safety story for retries.
days.drill: Explain why a retried POST can double-charge unless you have an idempotency key.
days.review: Networking page in the CS notes.
days.min60: Status codes plus the idempotency sentence.
days.hrs3: Draw the full request path from browser to app server. Add timeouts to the drawing.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one DP with a recurrence comment, 30 minutes.
days.second: Create a tiny orders and users example. Write: join, filter, group by with having, and one window function (row_number or sum over partition). Explain an index as a structure that speeds reads and costs writes. Composite index column order matters.
days.drill: Write the join without looking.
days.hrs3: Window function plus a paragraph on when an index is useless (leading-column mismatch, function wrapped on the column).

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Maintenance: one heap or interval problem, 25 minutes.
days.second: ACID in your own words. Isolation anomalies you can name: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, and the practical punchline that 'serializable is safer and often slower'. Mention row locks versus optimistic version columns. You are not implementing a database.
days.drill: Give one example of a lost update on a balance.
days.hrs3: Read a DDIA passage on replication lag and write five lines on read-your-writes.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: No coding maintenance today. Use the time on systems.
days.second: Cache aside versus write-through, named only. TTL, stampede, and the question 'what is the source of truth?'. Then read a RAG paper summary: retrieve documents, stuff them into the prompt, generate. Write three weaknesses the original setup has, using what you already know about chunks and hybrid search.
days.drill: Define cache aside.
days.hrs3: Full caching page and three weaknesses tied to chunks, citations, and evals.

days.week_title: The CS that design rounds quietly require
days.coding: Explain, out loud, without notes: index, transaction, retry with idempotency, lock. Then one coding redo.
days.second: Story seed 8: user-visible impact. Who had a better day because of the change, and how you know.
days.drill: Two of the four spoken explanations.
days.review: Record gaps in the CS page headings.
days.hrs3: All four explanations, one redo, story seed 8.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: One maintenance medium, 30 minutes, from a weak pattern.
days.second: Write your agenda on a card: (1) clarify functional requirements and non-goals, (2) scale sketch, (3) API, (4) data model, (5) high-level path, (6) the bottleneck you will actually go deep on, (7) tradeoffs and failure. Practice it on 'design a URL shortener' for 35 minutes without looking at a solution.
days.drill: Run steps 1–4 only, out loud.
days.hrs3: Full 35-minute pass plus a written scale sketch: reads per second, writes per second, storage for five years. Label every number as an assumption.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: No new coding pattern.
days.second: Blank redo of the shortener. Go deep on key generation (random versus counter), redirect latency, and cache. Mention analytics as a non-goal unless asked. Say what you would shard if writes grew.
days.drill: Draw only the read path.
days.review: systems/url-shortener.md with assumptions at the top.
days.hrs3: Full redo and a paragraph on how you would add 'similar URL' semantic lookup without putting a model on the redirect path.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: One maintenance problem, 25 minutes.
days.second: Token bucket versus sliding window, in words and a sketch. Where it runs: API gateway, per user and per IP. What you store. How clocks and multiple limiter nodes drift. Return 429. This design is also how you protect an LLM endpoint from a runaway client.
days.drill: Speak token bucket refill.
days.hrs3: Add a second key: limit by user and a stricter global limit for an expensive model route.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: None.
days.second: Design a paste service. Metadata in a database, body in object storage once past a size threshold, cache hot pastes, expiry. Mention virus scanning only if you have time. The point is separating metadata from blobs.
days.drill: Name the source of truth for the paste body.
days.hrs3: Add CDN for reads and a note on cache invalidation when a paste is deleted.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Build a small estimation card: seconds in a day, QPS from daily active users and actions, storage as rows times bytes times replication. Practice one estimate, then change a constraint when an imaginary interviewer says 'make it 10x' and show what breaks first.
days.drill: One QPS estimate on paper.
days.hrs3: The 10x follow-up on the paste service.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: None during the mock.
days.second: 40 minutes: design a rate limiter or the shortener, out loud, agenda card only. Retro: did you skip requirements, did you invent numbers, did you go deep on one bottleneck or draw fifteen boxes?
days.drill: Mock. Five-line retro.
days.hrs3: Mock, retro, and a 15-minute redraw of the weakest section.

days.week_title: A design method, then three small systems
days.coding: No coding.
days.second: Tell story 1 and story 6 in two minutes each. Record yourself or sit with a friend. Cut the preamble. End on the result.
days.drill: One story, two minutes.
days.review: Note the sentences you will delete.
days.hrs3: Both stories plus a rewritten opening line for each.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: One maintenance medium.
days.second: Design a simplified home feed. Celebrity problem: fan-out-on-write is painful for a user with millions of followers, so mix strategies. Ranking can be a later section; do not open with machine learning. Storage for posts versus storage for timelines.
days.drill: Define fan-out-on-write in two sentences.
days.hrs3: Add a sentence on where a ranking model would sit, and what happens when it times out: show a chronological fallback.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: 1:1 chat. Message table, inbox per user, online delivery via a connection, offline via stored messages. Read receipts as optional. Ordering per conversation. Media goes to blob storage. Presence is a separate small path.
days.drill: Draw the send path for one message.
days.hrs3: Group chat fan-out and a note on why 'exactly once' display is usually idempotent message ids.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Design notifications: event in, preference check, fan out to email, push, and in-app. Retries, dead letter, user-level rate limits so you do not mail someone fifty times. This is a queue problem wearing a product costume.
days.drill: Name the queue and the idempotency key.
days.hrs3: Add a digest mode: collapse bursts into one message.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: Build a one-page menu you can pull out in any design: leader/follower replication, async lag, quorums in words, conflict on a counter versus a document, outbox pattern so you do not dual-write to a database and a queue by hope. Pick the feed and say what can be stale.
days.drill: Explain read-your-writes for the person who just posted.
days.min60: The outbox idea in five sentences.
days.hrs3: Apply the menu to chat message send: what must be durable before you ack the sender.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: Design ingestion for a help-center bot: crawl, parse, chunk, embed, upsert with metadata, delete when a doc is unpublished. Query path: auth, embed question, filter by product and visibility, retrieve, optional rerank, prompt with citations, abstain if nothing clears a threshold. You are not choosing a vendor logo. You are naming responsibilities.
days.drill: Draw ingest only.
days.hrs3: Full query path and a failure: the doc changed and the index is stale. How does the user see freshness?

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: None.
days.second: 40 minutes: chat or notifications, agenda card, out loud. Retro aimed at one question: did failure and retries show up before the interviewer asked?
days.drill: Mock.
days.hrs3: Mock and a redraw of the failure path.

days.week_title: Feeds, chat, notifications, consistency
days.coding: No coding.
days.second: Two-minute tellings. Story 2 is the incident. Story 3 is the disagreement. Check that story 3 does not insult the other person.
days.drill: One story.
days.hrs3: Both, plus a note on which leadership theme each one proves.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One maintenance problem so coding does not go cold.
days.problems: One medium from the pattern index.
days.second: Pick a corpus you may store: your own notes, a public-domain handbook, or twenty pages you write about a fake product. Write ten questions whose answers live in that corpus, and record the passage that should be retrieved. This golden set is the project. The model is not.
days.drill: Write five questions and their source passages.
days.hrs3: Ten questions. At least two should be traps: the words match the wrong section.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: None.
days.second: Chunk the corpus with the rule from Week 7. Embed chunks. For each question, embed it and rank chunks by cosine. Print the top three. Use a brute-force scan if the corpus is small, and say that a real index replaces the scan.
days.drill: One question, top three printed.
days.review: Commit the script and a sample run.
days.hrs3: All ten questions printed. Note which trap questions failed.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Score hit@3: was the labeled passage in the top three? Write the misses in a table with a suspected reason: bad chunk boundary, synonym, too-broad chunk, or tie. Do not 'fix' by changing the label to match the model.
days.drill: Score five questions.
days.min60: A written hit@3 on five questions.
days.hrs3: All ten, plus a one-line fix you will try tomorrow (overlap, heading-based split, or a metadata field).

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: None.
days.second: Apply exactly one retrieval change. Re-run the same ten questions. Report the new hit@3 next to the old one. If it got worse, keep the note; negative results are interview gold.
days.drill: Ship the one change.
days.min60: The change and a partial rescore.
days.hrs3: Full rescore and a paragraph a hiring manager could read.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Add a metadata field such as product or visibility. Show a query that must not return a chunk from the wrong product even if the vector is close. This is the access-control lesson from Week 7, in code.
days.drill: One filtered query.
days.review: Document the filter in the README.
days.hrs3: A test that fails if the wrong product appears in the top three.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: No new features.
days.second: Five-minute spoken walkthrough: corpus, chunking, embedding, ranking, metric, the change you tried, what you would do at a million documents (ANN index, reranker, hybrid for error codes). Record it.
days.drill: Speak it once, messy.
days.hrs3: A clean take and a diagram.

days.week_title: Embeddings you can measure
days.coding: One timed medium, 35 minutes.
days.second: Story seed 9: an improvement nobody assigned. Initiative without chaos. What you noticed, what you changed, how you checked it was better.
days.drill: The story seed in four lines.
days.hrs3: Story plus the timed medium.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Take the top chunks and a question. Prompt the model to answer only from those chunks and to quote the chunk id it used. If the chunks are irrelevant, it must say it does not know. Save the prompt in git.
days.drill: One question end to end with a citation.
days.hrs3: Five questions. Mark any answer that used knowledge not in the chunks.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: None.
days.second: Add five questions whose answers are not in the corpus. A correct system refuses. A system that invents a confident answer fails, even if the prose is lovely. Tune the prompt or a similarity threshold until at least some of these refuse. Record what you changed.
days.drill: One out-of-corpus question refuses.
days.hrs3: Five out-of-corpus questions scored.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: One maintenance problem.
days.second: Expand to twenty questions: some factual, some that need two chunks, some traps, some out of corpus. Score faithfulness (did it stick to the text) separately from retrieval hit. A retrieved right passage with a wrong summary is a generation miss, not a vector miss.
days.drill: Score five more questions in the two-column way.
days.hrs3: All twenty scored in two columns.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: None.
days.second: Return the passage text, not only an id. If you cannot highlight the supporting sentence, do not claim a citation. Fix one unfaithful answer by changing the prompt or the context, then rescore only the affected rows.
days.drill: One answer with the passage attached.
days.hrs3: Rescore the unfaithful rows and write whether the fix was prompt, chunk, or retrieval.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.theme: Hybrid or rerank, one of them
days.coding: None.
days.second: If your misses are exact codes or names, add a simple lexical overlap score and merge it with cosine. If your misses are 'right documents, wrong order', add a rerank step even if the reranker is just a cross-encoder you call on five chunks, or a model asked to pick the best chunk. One of these, not a platform rewrite.
days.drill: Implement the merge or the rerank on a single query.
days.hrs3: Rescore the miss list only, and keep the change if the score improved.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: No features.
days.second: Eight-minute talk: retrieval metric, generation metric, refusal, the change that helped, what you would not trust this demo to do in production (privacy, freshness, adversarial users). Production honesty is an SDE-2 signal.
days.drill: Speak the 'would not ship' paragraph.
days.hrs3: Full eight minutes, recorded.

days.week_title: RAG with citations, abstention, and a real eval
days.coding: Fix one real bug in the RAG script. That counts as engineering practice.
days.problems: None from LeetCode unless the script is already solid.
days.second: Tell stories 8 and 9 in two minutes. Map each to a company theme you care about: Google's collaboration and ambiguity, Amazon's ownership and customer obsession, Meta's impact and move-fast-with-stability.
days.drill: One story mapped to one theme.
days.review: A theme tag on each story.
days.hrs3: Both stories and the bug fix committed.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: One timed medium.
days.second: Define one tool, for example a fake order-status function that reads a local dict. Send the tool schema to the model, execute the call yourself, send the result back, and get a final answer. Log every message. You own the loop.
days.drill: One tool round-trip logged.
days.hrs3: A second tool, plus a test where the model should not call a tool (a chit-chat question).

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: None.
days.second: Rebuild only the retrieval chain in LangChain or LCEL: loader or your chunks, retriever, prompt, model. Then write a note: what it shortened, what it hid, and one place you would drop it (tight latency, simple script, confusing stack traces during an incident). Knowing when not to use it is the SDE-2 answer.
days.drill: The chain runs one question.
days.review: The judgment note in the README.
days.min60: Chain plus the start of the note.
days.hrs3: Chain, note, and a comparison of logs versus your raw script.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: One timed medium from a different pattern than yesterday.
days.second: Model the bot as a graph. State: question, documents, tool result, draft, citations. Nodes: retrieve, grade or abstain, tool, answer. Edges: if documents are weak, abstain; if the question needs order status, call the tool; else answer from docs. Checkpointing means you can resume; say that, and turn it on only if the API is painless.
days.drill: Draw the graph on paper before installing anything.
days.hrs3: The graph handles answer, abstain, and one tool.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: None.
days.second: Add one interrupt: if the tool would 'refund' or otherwise mutate state, stop and require an explicit yes in the terminal. Even a fake refund teaches the production idea. Multi-agent swarms are out of scope; write one sentence on why a single graph with tools is your default.
days.drill: The interrupt triggers once.
days.hrs3: Interrupt plus the anti-swarm sentence.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: None.
days.second: Read what the Model Context Protocol is: a standard way for a host to give a model tools and data sources. You do not need to write a server unless you want a stretch. You do need to say how it differs from a one-off function call: discovery and reuse across hosts. Note the trust issue: a tool is code execution with extra steps, so you treat tool descriptions as untrusted input.
days.drill: Write the definition in five lines.
days.hrs3: Definition plus a threat you would actually mitigate: a tool that returns text telling the model to ignore the policy. Your mitigation is to keep system instructions and tool output in separate roles and to validate tool arguments. Do not build an attack.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: No new nodes.
days.second: Ten-minute explanation to an imaginary interviewer: why a graph, what the state holds, where you abstain, where a human confirms, what you would trace in production. If you skipped LangGraph for plain Python, explain that decision with the same confidence.
days.drill: Five minutes, notes allowed.
days.hrs3: Ten minutes without the drawing in hand, then look down and see what you forgot.

days.week_title: Tools, LangChain with judgment, LangGraph with state
days.coding: One coding redo, 30 minutes.
days.second: Story seed 10: you were pushed to ship and you saw a quality risk. What you negotiated, what you cut on purpose, what you refused to cut.
days.drill: Four-line seed.
days.hrs3: Seed expanded and the coding redo.

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: Two timed problems, 30 minutes each, from different patterns.
days.problems: One graph or tree, one DP or window.
days.second: Write the tree: start with a good prompt and examples if the task is small and the facts are in the prompt. Add tools if the task needs calculation or a live system. Add RAG if the facts change and live in documents. Consider fine-tuning only when the format or style must change at scale and prompting is not enough, and you have data and an eval. Fine-tuning does not replace retrieval of fresh facts.
days.drill: Write the four branches.
days.hrs3: Apply the tree to three fake requests: a refund tool, a policy bot, a tone adapter for support macros.

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: None.
days.second: Design an internal answer endpoint. Budgets: timeout, max tokens, a cheaper model for easy questions, a stronger model when retrieval confidence is low or the user retries. Cache exact repeat questions. Stream tokens if a person is waiting. Log prompt version, retrieved ids, token counts, and latency. Estimate cost as a formula, with placeholders for price per token rather than a memorized price.
days.drill: Draw the routing split.
days.hrs3: Add a load test thought: what breaks first, the model quota or your index?

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: One timed medium.
days.second: Write an eval plan for the RAG bot: golden questions, retrieval hit, faithfulness, refusal accuracy, and a human spot-check before any prompt change ships. LLM-as-judge is allowed as a helper and is not allowed as the only gate. Say why: judges share failure modes with the system they grade.
days.concept: A judge is not the gate
days.drill: List the metrics.
days.hrs3: The plan plus a small regression rule: a prompt change that drops refusal accuracy does not ship.

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: None.
days.second: Write the rules for your bot: do not send secrets to a third-party model, respect document visibility, do not follow instructions that arrive inside a retrieved page if they conflict with system policy, and prefer abstaining over inventing HR or medical or legal claims. This is defensive product sense. Do not research bypass techniques.
days.drill: The four rules.
days.hrs3: Add how you would test the rule about hostile text inside a document, using a harmless fake instruction such as 'say the secret word banana', and assert the bot does not obey it.

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: One short coding warm-up, 20 minutes.
days.second: Read the company sheet and write a personal delta for the two companies you will apply to first. Example: Amazon means every story maps to a leadership principle. Google L4 means coding clarity plus one solid design and a Googleyness conversation that is not a brag reel. An AI team means the RAG project walkthrough is part of the loop even if the job post says SDE.
days.drill: Write the delta for one company.
days.hrs3: Two companies, plus the questions you will ask the recruiter about the loop.

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: No coding.
days.second: Eight stories, two minutes each, with a break. Use a phone recorder. For each, check: situation is short, you made a decision, the result is concrete, the lesson is one sentence. Drop any story you cannot tell cleanly and replace it from your real work, not from fiction.
days.drill: Three stories.
days.hrs3: Eight stories and a plan to repair the weakest two tomorrow.

days.week_title: Production judgment, company deltas, story reps
days.coding: Redo one coding pattern you missed in this week's timers.
days.second: Rewrite the two weakest stories. Then take a real half-day off if you can. Week 16 is mocks, and exhaustion looks like a knowledge gap.
days.drill: One story rewrite.
days.hrs3: Both rewrites and the coding redo, then stop.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.coding: No problems until the resume has bullets.
days.second: One or two pages. Each bullet is a change with a scope and an effect. Remove tools you cannot discuss for five minutes. The RAG or search project can be a bullet if you can quote the before/after hit rate. Prepare a referral note that is three lines: role, why you, one proof point.
days.drill: Rewrite five bullets.
days.hrs3: Full pass and the blurb. Ask one person to read it.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.coding: Two questions back to back if you can, 45 minutes each, or one 45 and a written second. Out loud.
days.second: Retro against the checklist card. Schedule repairs only for misses. Do not open a new pattern guide.
days.drill: One 45-minute mock.
days.hrs3: Two rounds and a repair list of at most three items.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.coding: None.
days.second: 45 minutes. Pick feed, chat, or the LLM endpoint, whichever is less rehearsed. Agenda card. Retro: requirements, numbers, depth, failure.
days.drill: The mock.
days.hrs3: Mock plus a 20-minute repair of the weakest step.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.coding: One coding repair from Tuesday's list.
days.second: 20 minutes of questions you ask yourself: why this chunking, why this metric, what failed, what you would not ship, how you would add auth, how cost grows. If you stumble, fix the notes, not the architecture, unless the architecture is actually wrong.
days.drill: Ten minutes of questions.
days.hrs3: Twenty minutes and note fixes.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.coding: None.
days.second: 30 minutes of stories, then an application block: two companies, tailored bullets if needed, referral sent or a note in the tracker if you do not have a referral. Cold applications still count. Record the date, the role, the loop shape you were told, and the next action.
days.drill: One application fully submitted or ready.
days.hrs3: Two applications and a 30-minute story round.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.coding: 45-minute coding.
days.second: Then 30-minute design and 15-minute story, with five-minute breaks. This is the closest you get to a loop without an interviewer. Write energy notes: where you rushed, where you went silent.
days.drill: Coding plus one story.
days.hrs3: The full mini-loop.

days.week_title: Mocks, applications, and a weak-area budget
days.theme: Gap budget and stop adding topics
days.coding: Only if a gap is a coding pattern. Otherwise no new problems.
days.second: List at most five remaining gaps. Give each a date. Everything else is out of this cycle. Plan the next two weeks of applications on the tracker. Reread the decision tree and the agenda card once.
days.drill: Write the five gaps.
days.hrs3: The list, the next two weeks of applications, and an evening off.

topics.why: Loops grade clarity under a timer. Switching languages costs fluency you needed for edge cases.
topics.good: You clarify, give examples, name brute force, improve, code, and test without being prompted.
topics.practice: Week 0 diagnostic and every timed day after.
topics.resources: Your language tour; a personal checklist card.
topics.mistakes: Coding in silence, or starting to type before examples.

topics.why: Every coding round asks time and space, including follow-ups that change constraints.
topics.good: You state time, extra space, and one bottleneck before the interviewer asks.
topics.resources: A short algorithms chapter on asymptotics.
topics.mistakes: Confusing worst case with what one test input did.

topics.subtopic: Pattern notes and a mistake log
topics.why: SDE-2 prep fails by solving two hundred problems and retaining twenty.
topics.good: Each problem is filed under a trigger phrase, with the bug you actually hit.
topics.resources: A git repo, not a highlighter.
topics.mistakes: Saving links instead of writing the invariant.

topics.why: The most common first screen.
topics.good: You reach for a map when you need a complement, a count, or a grouping, and you say expected O(1) lookup.
topics.resources: NeetCode arrays and hashing, or Blind 75.
topics.mistakes: Nested loops after you already named the map solution.

topics.why: Turns repeated scanning into a linear preprocess.
topics.good: You handle the empty-prefix boundary and the 'store how often this prefix was seen' variant.
topics.mistakes: Off-by-one on the left edge.

topics.why: Sorted arrays and in-place edits.
topics.good: You name the invariant before moving a pointer.
topics.mistakes: Moving both pointers without a rule.

topics.why: Substring and subarray questions, often the medium on a phone screen.
topics.good: You know whether you want the longest or the shortest valid window.
topics.mistakes: Recomputing the window from scratch each time.

topics.why: Parsing, next-greater, and histogram-style follow-ups.
topics.good: You can draw the stack for nested input and explain one pop.
topics.mistakes: Using a stack because the chapter said so, not because of LIFO.

topics.why: Level order and fairness.
topics.good: You can implement a queue and explain amortized cost.
topics.mistakes: Using a list as a queue from the front in a hot loop without comment.

topics.why: Pointer accuracy. Interviewers watch for lost tails and nulls.
topics.good: You draw arrows and use a dummy head on purpose.
topics.mistakes: Converting every list to an array to avoid pointers.

topics.why: Off-by-one here predicts off-by-one in design estimates and in code.
topics.good: One bound convention, tested on an even-length array.
topics.mistakes: Changing the loop condition halfway through the problem.

topics.why: A frequent 'medium that feels like math' pattern.
topics.good: You state the predicate 'is X enough?' before coding.
topics.mistakes: Searching indexes when the search space is the answer.

topics.why: A core L4 coding topic.
topics.good: Inorder, preorder, postorder, and level order, one of them iterative.
topics.mistakes: Forgetting to snapshot the level size in BFS.

topics.why: Validation and search.
topics.good: You pass min and max bounds down the recursion.
topics.mistakes: Only comparing a node to its parent.

topics.why: Path-sum and construction problems.
topics.good: You know when the path list must be copied or popped.
topics.mistakes: Sharing one list across branches without backtracking.

topics.why: Streaming and 'keep the best k'.
topics.good: You know your language's heap order and when a full sort is fine.
topics.mistakes: Building a heap of all n when k is tiny, without saying why.

topics.why: Disguised graph problems.
topics.good: Visited is marked at enqueue time, and you can say why.
topics.mistakes: Marking visited too late and doubling work.

topics.why: Object graphs, not only matrices.
topics.good: A map from old node to new node doubles as visited.
topics.mistakes: Infinite recursion on a cycle.

topics.why: Dependency and course-schedule questions, and a design concept for build systems and workflows.
topics.good: You detect a cycle with Kahn's algorithm.
topics.mistakes: Forgetting to reduce indegree.

topics.why: Connectivity and redundant edges.
topics.good: Find with compression, union by rank or size.
topics.mistakes: Using it for shortest paths.

topics.why: Distance from many starts.
topics.good: All sources enter the queue before BFS begins.
topics.mistakes: Looping single-source BFS and taking a min.

topics.why: Weighted graphs show up as a follow-up more than as the whole round.
topics.good: You can say 'priority queue of distance' and when a plain BFS is enough (unweighted).
topics.mistakes: Dijkstra on a graph with negative edges.

topics.why: The pattern that most self-taught candidates postpone until it is too late.
topics.good: The comment says what dp[i] means before any loop.
topics.mistakes: Coding a table you cannot define.

topics.why: Take/skip and unbounded reuse.
topics.good: You can say whether an item may be reused and what that does to loop order.
topics.mistakes: Memorizing loop order with no meaning.

topics.why: Decode, word break, subsequences.
topics.good: n^2 LIS is the one you can code; n log n is a follow-up you can describe.
topics.mistakes: Starting with the clever LIS method.

topics.why: Paths, LCS, edit distance.
topics.good: You fill a small table by hand first.
topics.mistakes: Wrong base row on edit distance.

topics.why: Calendar and meeting questions, and a greedy instinct.
topics.good: You know whether you sorted by start or by end, and why.
topics.mistakes: A DP solution for a greedy problem.

topics.why: Decision trees. Also the mental model for search in AI agents.
topics.good: Choose, explore, unchoose, drawn once for a tiny input.
topics.mistakes: Forgetting to pop the choice.

topics.why: Autocomplete designs and word search follow-ups.
topics.good: Insert and search, plus the difference between a stored word and a prefix.
topics.mistakes: A hash set of every prefix when they asked for a trie.

topics.why: A minority of rounds, usually one trick.
topics.good: Single Number explained with pairs canceling.
topics.mistakes: Spending a week on bit tricks while DP is shaky.

topics.subtopic: Prove the choice or don't ship it
topics.why: Interviewers ask why this local choice is safe.
topics.good: You can name the sort key and a counterexample to the wrong key.
topics.practice: Non-overlapping intervals and one scheduling problem.
topics.mistakes: Calling every optimization greedy.

topics.why: Some loops and many RRK chats still wander into class design.
topics.good: Entities, relationships, and one extension, in an hour.
topics.mistakes: A week of design-pattern flashcards.

topics.why: Occasionally the whole problem, often a corner.
topics.good: You mention overflow, integer division, and modulo when the prompt smells like it.
topics.practice: Only if mocks expose a gap.
topics.mistakes: A number-theory side quest.

topics.why: Design and debugging rounds assume this.
topics.good: Deadlock example with two locks. Race explained on a counter.
topics.resources: OS interview notes at chapter depth, not a textbook cover-to-cover.
topics.mistakes: Kernel trivia.

topics.why: Lets you reject impossible designs politely.
topics.good: You use a labeled approximation table and change the design when a number is absurd.
topics.resources: A latency-number cheat sheet you wrote.
topics.mistakes: Quoting nanoseconds as if they were exact on every CPU.

topics.why: Every backend loop.
topics.good: You can draw a request and name timeouts, retries, and status codes you would return.
topics.resources: A networking chapter aimed at interviews.
topics.mistakes: Reciting the OSI model instead of the request path.

topics.why: Design rounds are API rounds in disguise.
topics.good: POST versus PUT, 409 versus 400, idempotency keys on retries.
topics.practice: Rate limiter and URL shortener APIs.
topics.mistakes: APIs with no error model.

topics.why: Practical screens and many take-homes.
topics.good: You write a join and explain a composite index's column order.
topics.mistakes: An index on every column.

topics.why: Correctness stories in design.
topics.good: Lost update example. What serializable buys and costs.
topics.mistakes: ACID as four adjectives you cannot illustrate.

topics.why: Almost every design.
topics.good: You name the source of truth and what happens on a miss storm.
topics.mistakes: A cache with no invalidation story.

topics.why: Senior-leaning follow-up even at SDE-2.
topics.good: You do not size a CPU pool at 200 threads and call it done.
topics.practice: A paragraph in the CS notes.
topics.mistakes: Equating async and multithreaded.

topics.why: Stops the 'fifteen boxes' failure mode.
topics.good: Requirements and one deep bottleneck happen before you run out of time.
topics.mistakes: Starting with the database logo.

topics.subtopic: QPS and storage you can revise
topics.why: Interviewers change the constraint to see you think.
topics.good: Assumptions are written, and you know what breaks at 10x.
topics.mistakes: False precision.

topics.why: The warm-up design everyone still botches under time.
topics.good: Key strategy and read path are explicit.
topics.resources: A classic write-up, then a blank redo.
topics.mistakes: Base62 trivia with no cache story.

topics.why: Protects APIs, including model endpoints.
topics.good: Limit key, storage, and 429 behavior.
topics.mistakes: A single global counter with no burst policy.

topics.why: Object storage versus database.
topics.good: Bodies do not live in the relational row once they are large.
topics.mistakes: Storing megabytes in the primary database without comment.

topics.why: The standard 'it depends' design.
topics.good: You mix fan-out strategies and have a fallback if ranking fails.
topics.mistakes: Opening with a model instead of the timeline.

topics.why: Messaging shows up constantly.
topics.good: Online path, stored path, message ids for idempotency.
topics.mistakes: Exactly-once as a slogan.

topics.why: Fan-out with product constraints.
topics.good: Preference checks and a cap so you cannot spam a user.
topics.mistakes: A queue with no dead-letter story.

topics.why: The follow-up after the happy path.
topics.good: You can point at what is allowed to be stale.
topics.mistakes: Dual-writing to a database and a queue with hope.

topics.why: Scale follow-ups.
topics.good: You notice a celebrity key, a hot partition, or a clock-based id collision risk.
topics.practice: A section in the consistency notes.
topics.mistakes: Consistent hashing as a magic word with no picture.

topics.why: Bridges DSA and design.
topics.good: Prefix structure, top suggestions, and a cache.
topics.mistakes: A trie with no update story.

topics.why: SDE-2 is judged on scope, not only on algorithms. Amazon maps every round to principles. Google listens for collaboration and humility.
topics.good: A short situation, a decision, a concrete result, a one-sentence lesson.
topics.resources: Your own career. Leadership principle pages only as a checklist after the story exists.
topics.mistakes: Fiction, or a story where the team is the villain.

topics.why: The level signal is that you improve work beyond a ticket you were handed.
topics.good: At least two stories show cross-team effect, mentoring, or an unassigned fix.
topics.mistakes: Only solo heroics.

topics.why: Google's loop includes collaboration, ambiguity, and sometimes role-related knowledge, then a hiring committee you never meet.
topics.good: You answer like a teammate. You do not recite values.
topics.mistakes: A prepared speech.

topics.subtopic: Stories mapped after they are true
topics.why: The bar raiser is real. Unmapped stories hurt.
topics.good: Each principle you claim has a story with a decision.
topics.mistakes: Inventing a story to fit a principle.

topics.why: Failures without ownership sound like excuses. Conflicts without respect sound like you are hard to hire.
topics.good: You name your part and the change that followed.
topics.mistakes: Blame.

topics.why: Senior candidates are graded on judgment here too, and SDE-2 is close.
topics.good: You ask how they review model or design changes, and what oncall looks like.
topics.mistakes: Asking only about perks.

topics.subtopic: Bullets you can defend for five minutes
topics.why: The resume chooses the stories the interviewer will pull.
topics.good: Scope, action, effect. No tool you cannot discuss.
topics.mistakes: Keyword stuffing.

topics.why: Untimed study overstates your level.
topics.good: A written retro with one repair, starting Week 7.
topics.mistakes: Collecting mock scores without repairing.

topics.subtopic: Recruiter, screens, onsite, committee, team match
topics.why: Google in particular does not end at the onsite. Offers follow committee and team matching.
topics.good: You know the stages for your two target companies and you ask the recruiter to confirm.
topics.mistakes: Assuming a blog post from 2019 is the loop.

topics.subtopic: Level, competing timelines, what you want
topics.why: SDE-2 bands are wide. The skill is knowing the process, not bluffing a number you found on a forum.
topics.good: You ask level, scope, and timeline. You do not accept in the same breath as the first verbal offer if you have a real question.
topics.practice: Read once before you need it.
topics.resources: levels.fyi for current public bands, checked the month you interview.
topics.mistakes: A script that treats negotiation as a fight.

topics.why: Searching feels productive and is not the same as being in process.
topics.good: Every target has a status and a next action.
topics.mistakes: Twenty tabs of job posts and zero submissions.

topics.why: Stops magical thinking in design rounds.
topics.good: You can explain training versus inference and why the model does not know your wiki.
topics.resources: Karpathy's Intro to LLMs, or any equivalent current talk.
topics.mistakes: Saying the model 'looks up' facts.

topics.why: Cost, latency, and chunking are all in tokens.
topics.good: You explain BPE in two minutes and treat token counts as the budget.
topics.resources: A BPE explainer and a tokenizer preview.
topics.mistakes: Equating words and tokens.

topics.why: You will be asked why the bot is flaky.
topics.good: You know what to lower when you need stable structured output.
topics.mistakes: Turning temperature up to 'make it smarter'.

topics.why: The cheapest iteration, and the easiest to overclaim.
topics.good: Every prompt you keep is in git and has at least a tiny eval.
topics.mistakes: Prompt poetry with no test set.

topics.why: Tools and evaluators need parseable results.
topics.good: You can ask for a schema and validate it, with a retry or a fallback.
topics.practice: Add a schema to one tool call in Week 14.
topics.mistakes: Regex on paragraphs.

topics.why: Enough to talk to researchers and to read traces. Not a from-scratch trainer.
topics.good: One block from memory: attention, residual, feed-forward, norm. Q, K, V roles.
topics.mistakes: Derivations you cannot finish under interview stress.

topics.why: Candidates jump to fine-tuning.
topics.good: You say fine-tuning changes style or format, not the company's fresh facts.
topics.resources: A short fine-tuning overview. LoRA by name only.
topics.mistakes: Fine-tuning to avoid building retrieval.

topics.why: The retrieval primitive.
topics.good: You compute or call embeddings and rank by cosine.
topics.mistakes: Assuming a higher cosine always means a correct answer.

topics.why: You should know what the index is approximating.
topics.good: You can implement cosine for tiny vectors without a library.
topics.mistakes: Normalizing twice and not noticing.

topics.why: The standard two-stage stack.
topics.good: You can say why you do not cross-encode the whole corpus.
topics.mistakes: Reranking a million vectors online.

topics.why: How vector databases stay fast.
topics.good: You define them as approximate, with a recall cost.
topics.mistakes: Promising exact neighbors from an ANN index.

topics.why: Choosing a home for vectors.
topics.good: You pick based on filters, scale, and what you already operate, not on a trend.
topics.resources: Docs for one engine you actually run, plus names of two others.
topics.mistakes: Running three databases in a tutorial.

topics.why: The silent killer of RAG demos.
topics.good: You can name a failure mode your own corpus hit.
topics.mistakes: One global chunk size with no inspection.

topics.why: Multi-tenant products fail here.
topics.good: A test shows the wrong tenant cannot be retrieved.
topics.mistakes: Asking the model not to mention secrets that are sitting in the prompt.

topics.why: Exact codes, SKUs, and names.
topics.good: You tell the error-code story.
topics.mistakes: Semantic-only search for identifiers.

topics.why: The design round for AI teams.
topics.good: Crawl, chunk, embed, upsert, filter, retrieve, optional rerank, cite, abstain.
topics.mistakes: A single box labeled AI.

topics.why: Trust.
topics.good: Answers point at text a person can read.
topics.mistakes: A citation id that does not match the claim.

topics.why: A bot that always answers will fail a good interviewer.
topics.good: You measure refusal, not only happy-path accuracy.
topics.mistakes: A threshold you never tested.

topics.why: The difference between a demo and a project.
topics.good: A table with hit rate and faithfulness, before and after one change.
topics.resources: Your eval.md. RAGAS only after the table exists, if you want a named tool.
topics.mistakes: Changing labels to make the demo look right.

topics.why: You need vocabulary: invented fact, wrong citation, ignored context.
topics.good: You can classify a bad answer from your own log.
topics.mistakes: Using the word as a shrug.

topics.why: Stretch techniques when the raw question retrieves poorly.
topics.good: You know the names and the cost, and you try them only after chunking and hybrid are sane.
topics.practice: Reading, plus one experiment only if Week 13 misses justify it.
topics.mistakes: A stack of rewriters with no eval.

topics.why: Common on resumes and in codebases you may join.
topics.good: You rebuilt one chain and wrote where the framework hid a bug.
topics.mistakes: A resume full of LangChain with no raw-API experience.

topics.why: How teams ship agents that are inspectable.
topics.good: You can draw state and the abstain edge.
topics.mistakes: A swarm of agents for a one-tool bot.

topics.why: Agents are tool loops.
topics.good: You implemented the loop once without a framework.
topics.mistakes: Letting the model pretend it called the tool.

topics.why: Production agents that refund or delete need a person.
topics.good: One mutating tool pauses for confirmation.
topics.mistakes: Auto-running side effects because the demo was smoother.

topics.why: A 2025–2026 interface you will be asked about.
topics.good: You define host, tool, and the trust boundary in five lines.
topics.mistakes: A custom server before you can explain a function call.

topics.why: Reason-and-act loops are useful and easy to overuse.
topics.good: Your default is an explicit graph. ReAct is a choice you can justify.
topics.practice: A paragraph next to the graph.
topics.mistakes: An unbounded loop with no step cap.

topics.why: Chat bots get this question immediately.
topics.good: You separate conversation window, retrieved docs, and long-term user memory, and you say which one you did not build.
topics.practice: A section of the Week 14 talk.
topics.mistakes: Stuffing the entire history into every call with no budget.

topics.why: You cannot eval what you cannot reconstruct.
topics.good: A log that lets you replay one bad answer.
topics.mistakes: Print statements with no prompt version.

topics.why: SDE-2 means you can run the feature on a budget.
topics.good: A formula for cost and a timeout story.
topics.resources: Provider pricing pages, read for the meters not the memorized prices.
topics.mistakes: A single giant model for every call.

topics.why: User-facing bots.
topics.good: You know why streaming exists and what you log when the user cancels.
topics.practice: A paragraph in the endpoint design.
topics.mistakes: Buffering the full answer and calling it streaming.

topics.why: Prompt instructions are not an access-control layer.
topics.good: Visibility filters happen before the model sees text.
topics.mistakes: A system prompt that says 'be safe' and nothing else.

topics.why: A basic production threat for RAG.
topics.good: You can describe a harmless test and a mitigation without building an attack.
topics.mistakes: Following orders that arrived in a PDF.

topics.why: Teams will ask how a prompt change ships.
topics.good: Refusal accuracy and faithfulness are gates, and an LLM judge is not the only gate.
topics.mistakes: Vibe checks.

topics.why: Cost follow-up.
topics.good: A rule for when the stronger model is invoked.
topics.mistakes: Routing with no fallback when the strong model errors.

topics.why: Ingestion is where RAG actually breaks.
topics.good: You can say what your parser loses: tables, headers, scanned pages.
topics.resources: Whatever parser you used, plus its limits in the README.
topics.mistakes: Assuming text extraction is solved.

topics.why: Docs change.
topics.good: Unpublishing a doc removes or hides its vectors.
topics.mistakes: An index that only grows.

topics.why: Some loops ask for recommendations at a high level even on LLM teams.
topics.good: You can place a model behind a timeout and a non-model fallback.
topics.resources: A single ML design primer, interview depth.
topics.mistakes: A training pipeline diagram when they asked for the serving path.

topics.why: You need a scoreboard.
topics.good: You report hit@k on a fixed set and you do not move labels.
topics.mistakes: Accuracy as a single vague percentage.

topics.why: Shipping criterion, not a policy appendix.
topics.good: You know what must not leave your network.
topics.mistakes: Pasting production data into a personal chatbot account.

topics.subtopic: Images and audio as later context
topics.why: So you are not surprised by the question.
topics.good: You can say you would embed or caption non-text, and that your project did not.
topics.mistakes: A new project in Week 16.

topics.subtopic: When relationships matter more than passages
topics.why: A stretch term in current write-ups.
topics.good: You know it builds a graph over entities and you do not need it for a help center.
topics.mistakes: Adopting it before hybrid search works.

companies.level: SDE-2 maps to L4 in most orgs. L3 is new grad / entry. L5 is senior. Confirm the req, because titles on the posting can lag the ladder.
companies.loop: Recruiter, one or two coding screens, then a full loop that often includes multiple coding rounds, one design round at L4, and a behavioral or Googleyness round. Role-related knowledge shows up for some teams. A hiring committee reviews the packet. Team matching is a separate stage. Offers do not happen in the last interview.
companies.coding: Medium problems, clean code, tests, and communication. Optimal or a clearly justified near-optimal. Graphs, trees, DP, and binary search are common. They care that you talk.
companies.design: One service. Requirements, estimates, data model, and one deep dive. Not 'design Google Search' from scratch unless you are interviewing for a search-infra niche, and even then they scope it.
companies.behavior: Collaboration, comfort with ambiguity, intellectual humility, user focus. Concrete stories. No culture-deck recital.
companies.ai: ML and Gemini-adjacent teams add a project deep dive or ML design. Still expect the coding bar. Be ready to discuss retrieval, evals, and privacy if the req mentions LLM features.
companies.surprise: The committee can downlevel or no-hire even after a friendly onsite. Team match can take longer than the interviews. Feedback is sparse.
companies.delta: Practice thinking aloud until it is boring. Prepare one design you can finish in 35 minutes. Ask the recruiter which round is design versus RRK.

companies.level: E4 is the usual SDE-2 equivalent. E5 is senior. E3 is entry.
companies.loop: Often a recruiter screen, a coding screen, then an onsite heavy on coding plus a design round and a behavioral round. Product sense is more central for product roles than for backend engineering, but impact still matters.
companies.coding: Fast, correct, conversational. Two questions in a round is common. Speed matters more than at Google, which punishes over-exploring.
companies.design: Practical and product-shaped: feed, chat, or a service the company obviously runs. State tradeoffs.
companies.behavior: Past impact, conflict, and working in ambiguity. They listen for what you personally did.
companies.ai: Ranking and integrity teams may ask how a model fails in production and how you would measure it. Retrieval projects help. Coding does not get waived.
companies.surprise: The pace. Candidates who narrate beautifully but finish one problem lose to candidates who finish two cleanly.
companies.delta: Timed sets of two mediums. A feed design you can redraw from blank.

companies.level: L5 is SDE-2. L4 is SDE-1. L6 is senior. This mapping surprises people coming from Google's numbering.
companies.loop: Recruiter, online assessment or phone coding depending on the org, then a loop that mixes coding, design, and leadership principles. A bar raiser is in the loop and is not your future teammate.
companies.coding: Correct and maintainable. They will still ask complexity. Object-oriented follow-ups happen.
companies.design: Working backwards from the customer. Availability and operational pain show up. Draw the failure path.
companies.behavior: Leadership principles in every round, including coding. Stories need ownership, a decision, and a metric or a clear customer effect.
companies.ai: Alexa, search, and AWS-adjacent orgs may ask how you evaluate a model feature and how you protect customer data. Map that to the same principles, especially ownership and earn trust.
companies.surprise: A brilliant coding round with weak stories is a no. The bar raiser is looking for a hole.
companies.delta: Write the principle next to each story after the story is true. Practice answering 'what did you do?' in the first thirty seconds.

companies.level: 62 is a common SDE-2 band, 61 often entry, 63–64 moving toward senior. Bands move; ask the recruiter.
companies.loop: Screen plus an onsite that mixes coding, design, and behavioral. The tone is often more collaborative than a pure speed screen. Some orgs include a practical or past-project review.
companies.coding: Solid mediums. They sometimes steer toward a hint if you talk well. Still finish the code.
companies.design: Service design with clear APIs. Azure-flavored teams may push on identity, storage choice, or cost.
companies.behavior: Growth mindset shows up as a real question: what you learned, how you handled feedback.
companies.ai: Copilot and Azure AI teams want RAG and evaluation literacy plus normal engineering. Be ready for a project walkthrough.
companies.surprise: Collaborative does not mean easy. Vague designs fail here too.
companies.delta: Prepare a feedback story. If the team is Azure, know the difference between a database and object storage in your own design, not as a product pitch.

companies.level: ICT3 is a typical mid-level match for SDE-2, ICT4 is senior. Team variance is high.
companies.loop: Team-specific. Often coding plus a deep dive into something you have built. Domain rounds are real: media, privacy, clients, or services depending on the group.
companies.coding: Can be practical, sometimes closer to real code than puzzle-only. Ask what the screen will be.
companies.design: Tied to the team's systems. Privacy and on-device constraints appear for some orgs.
companies.behavior: Craft, secrecy-aware collaboration, and how you work with hardware or design partners when that is the job.
companies.ai: On-device and privacy constraints change the RAG story: what is allowed to leave the device, what runs locally. Do not assume a cloud vector database is the answer.
companies.surprise: The loop you read about online may be a different org. The recruiter is the source of truth.
companies.delta: Reread the job post line by line and prepare one project story at a depth you can whiteboard.

companies.level: Titles are flat. Many engineering roles hire at a senior bar. SDE-2 candidates sometimes discover the scope is L5-like.
companies.loop: Fewer ceremonial rounds, more conversation with the team about judgment, past work, and a practical problem. Culture memo values are not a script, but freedom-and-responsibility shows up as 'did you exercise judgment?'.
companies.coding: May be present and may look like real debugging. Confirm.
companies.design: Tied to scale they actually run: streaming, recommendations, studio tooling. Operational maturity matters.
companies.behavior: Candor and ownership. Stories where you waited to be told what to do will fall flat.
companies.ai: Personalization teams care about metrics and offline versus online eval. A retrieval eval you can defend is more relevant than a framework tour.
companies.surprise: The level bar. If the conversations feel senior, they are.
companies.delta: Lead with judgment and measurement. If you are earlier than that, a different company may be the better SDE-2 target this cycle.

companies.level: L4 is a common mid-level, L5 senior. Confirm.
companies.loop: Coding, design, and behavioral. Marketplace and reliability stories resonate because the product is physical and real-time.
companies.design: Geolocation, dispatch, or a generic service with strong consistency thinking. They notice if you ignore failure.
companies.behavior: Impact under messy operations. Oncall and incident stories land well when they are true.
companies.ai: Matching and pricing teams may ask experiment design at a high level: what metric, what you would not ship on a bad eval.
companies.surprise: Hands-on follow-ups. 'What happens when this dependency times out?'
companies.delta: Bring the incident story and a design with an explicit timeout.

companies.level: Leveling is company-specific; ask. The craft bar is high relative to many SDE-2 postings.
companies.loop: Often includes practical debugging or an integration-style exercise, API design, coding, and a conversation about how you work. Read the latest candidate guidance they publish.
companies.coding: Correctness and API taste. Money movement means idempotency is not abstract.
companies.design: APIs, webhooks, retries, exactly the consistency menu from Week 11.
companies.behavior: Writing quality and user (developer) empathy. They may read something you wrote.
companies.ai: Support and risk teams use models carefully. Hallucinated answers about money are unacceptable. Your abstention metric matters.
companies.surprise: A practical round that does not look like LeetCode.
companies.delta: Practice reading unfamiliar code and writing a small, boring, well-tested API. Bring the idempotency story.

companies.level: Mid-level maps roughly to SDE-2; confirm the number on the ladder they are using.
companies.loop: Coding plus design plus cross-functional collaboration. They listen for how you work with design, trust, and ops.
companies.design: Marketplace, search, or booking. Double-booking and calendars are natural deep dives.
companies.behavior: Belonging and collaboration are easy to fake and easy to spot. Use a real disagreement story.
companies.ai: Search and support experiences. Retrieval quality and freshness of listings or policies.
companies.surprise: A design that ignores the two-sided marketplace.
companies.delta: One booking or calendar design, and story 3 rehearsed without a villain.

companies.company: AI labs and research-heavy product teams
companies.level: Titles vary wildly: member of technical staff, research engineer, software engineer. Read the posting for coding versus research ratio. Many 'engineer' seats still want SDE-2 coding plus a project.
companies.loop: Coding screen, project deep dive, and a practical discussion of evals or data. Some use take-homes. Research scientist loops are a different path and are not this plan.
companies.coding: Often still a normal coding screen. Do not skip Weeks 1–8 because the title says AI.
companies.design: An LLM system: ingest, retrieve, serve, evaluate, control cost. Sometimes a data pipeline.
companies.behavior: Taste: what you refused to ship, how you tested, how you handled ambiguous product goals.
companies.ai: This is the main event. Your Week 12–15 project, the decision tree, and the safety note are the packet.
companies.surprise: A practical session where they watch you change a prompt or an eval, or they ask you to read a short paper section.
companies.delta: The recorded walkthrough from Weeks 12–14. A one-page eval. Honesty about what the demo cannot do.

projects.name: Semantic search over a corpus you control
projects.outcome: Ten questions, labeled passages, hit@3 before and after one change, plus a metadata filter test.
projects.done_when: A stranger can run the script from the README and read eval.md without you narrating.
projects.steps: Golden set; chunk; embed; rank; score; change one thing; remeasure; add a wrong-tenant test; record a five-minute talk.

projects.name: Grounded RAG bot
projects.outcome: Cited answers or a refusal, scored on twenty questions split by retrieval and faithfulness.
projects.done_when: You can show an unfaithful answer you caught and the change that fixed or did not fix it.
projects.steps: Prompt in git; citations that include passage text; out-of-corpus refusals; two-column eval; one second stage if the misses justify it.

projects.name: Tool-using graph
projects.outcome: A raw tool loop and a LangGraph (or explicit Python) graph with abstain and a human confirm on a mutating tool.
projects.done_when: You can draw the state on a whiteboard and say where you would not use the framework.
projects.steps: Raw function call; LangChain retrieval chain plus a judgment note; graph; interrupt; MCP definition; ten-minute defense.

projects.name: Production pass
projects.outcome: Decision tree, endpoint design with cost formula, eval gates, privacy rules, and a harmless test for hostile retrieved text.
projects.done_when: You can tell an interviewer what you would not ship and how a prompt change gets rejected.
projects.steps: Decision tree on three fake requests; endpoint design; eval plan; safety note; company delta for two targets.

cheats.title: Coding round card
cheats.body:
1. Restate the problem and the constraints.
2. Give three examples: typical, empty or one element, and a sneaky case.
3. Name the brute force and its cost.
4. Name the better structure and its cost before coding.
5. Code in your one language. Talk while you type.
6. Run the examples by hand. Then one extra edge.
7. If you are stuck for five minutes, say what you know and what you are trying. Silence reads as stuckness.
8. Stop polishing names after the solution works. Use the last minutes on tests.

cheats.title: Pattern triggers
cheats.body:
Complement or pair in an unsorted array → hash map.
Sorted array and a pair or a palindrome → two pointers.
Contiguous subarray or substring with a validity rule → sliding window.
Nested structure that must close in order → stack.
Next greater or previous smaller → monotonic stack.
K-th or top-k or merge k sorted → heap.
Sorted or rotated or 'minimum X such that possible' → binary search.
Tree, parent pointers, or recursive structure → DFS/BFS, and bounds if it is a BST.
Grid of land or rooms → graph flood.
Dependencies or prerequisites → topological sort.
Dynamic connectivity → union-find.
Optimal substructure on prefixes → DP, but write the state in words first.
All combinations or permutations → backtracking.
Overlapping meetings → sort intervals.
Prefix dictionary → trie.
Single number among pairs → XOR.

cheats.title: Design agenda
cheats.body:
1. Functional requirements. Non-goals. Who is the user?
2. Scale sketch with assumptions written down. QPS, storage, retention.
3. API: main calls, auth, idempotency, error codes.
4. Data model: source of truth, indexes, what is cached.
5. Happy path drawing, few boxes.
6. Pick the bottleneck the constraints imply and go deep: shard, queue, cache, or consistency.
7. Failure: timeout, retry, duplicate delivery, hot key, dependency down.
8. If time remains: observability and one alternative you rejected.
When they change a number, say what breaks first. Do not redraw the entire diagram in a panic.

cheats.title: Estimation anchors
cheats.body:
These are planning anchors, not measurements of your laptop.
About 10^5 seconds in a day, so 1 million events per day is roughly 12 per second.
100 million events per day is roughly 1,200 per second.
Latency instincts, as orders of magnitude: memory is far cheaper than disk, disk is far cheaper than crossing a continent, and a chain of five network calls spends the budget of a user-facing request.
Storage: rows × average bytes × replication × retention. Say the assumption out loud.
If the answer must come back in tens of milliseconds, you do not have time for a cross-region quorum plus a large model plus a cold disk read. Say which one you will move.

cheats.title: Consistency menu
cheats.body:
At-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers is the honest default.
Exactly-once is a careful end-to-end property, not a checkbox on a queue.
Read-your-writes: the person who just posted should see the post. Followers can lag.
Outbox: write the business row and the outgoing event in the same database transaction, then publish. Do not dual-write and hope.
Retries need idempotency keys. Timeouts need a policy. Queues need dead letters.
A cache is not a source of truth. Name the source of truth in every design.

cheats.title: RAG checklist
cheats.body:
Ingest: parse, keep structure, chunk, attach metadata, embed, upsert, and delete when the source is unpublished.
Query: authenticate, embed the question, filter by visibility, retrieve, optionally rerank or fuse with lexical search, prompt only with those passages, cite the passage text, abstain when support is weak.
Evaluate retrieval separately from faithfulness. Include out-of-corpus questions.
Do not let the model be the access-control layer.
Exact identifiers (error codes, SKUs, names) need lexical or filter support, not embeddings alone.
One change at a time, then rescore the same questions.
Log prompt version, chunk ids, token counts, and latency so a bad answer is reconstructable.

cheats.title: Prompt, tools, RAG, or fine-tune
cheats.body:
Prompt and examples: the task is small and the facts fit in the window.
Tools: you need math, search, or a side effect in a real system. You execute the tool, not the model.
RAG: facts change, live in documents, and must be cited.
Fine-tune: format or style at scale, with data and an eval. It does not store this quarter's policy.
Human confirm: any tool that refunds, deletes, sends, or pays.
If you cannot say which branch you are on, you are not ready to pick a framework.

cheats.title: LangChain and LangGraph, the short version
cheats.body:
LangChain: loaders, splitters, retrievers, prompts, and chains. Useful when the boilerplate is the bottleneck. A liability when you cannot see the messages that were sent.
LCEL: a way to compose those steps. Know it as vocabulary. You do not need every helper.
LangGraph: an explicit state machine. Nodes are steps. Edges are decisions. State is the data you would otherwise hide in globals. Checkpoints let you resume or interrupt.
Default: one graph, a few tools, a step cap, an abstain edge, a human on mutations.
Skip the framework when the script is fifty lines and you are in an incident.

cheats.title: Vector index words
cheats.body:
Brute-force scan: exact, fine for thousands of vectors, too slow for millions per query.
HNSW: a graph of vectors, fast and approximate, uses memory.
IVF: clusters, search only some clusters, also approximate.
Index recall: did the index return the true nearest neighbors. Different phrase from 'did we retrieve the right document', which depends on chunking and the embedding model too.
Filters on tenant, language, and time belong in metadata. Apply them so the nearest neighbor cannot be a document the user must not see.
pgvector fits when Postgres is already the source of truth and scale is moderate. A dedicated engine fits when search is the product. A local library fits for the Week 12 project.

cheats.title: Behavioral skeleton
cheats.body:
Situation: one or two sentences of context.
Task: what you, not the team, were responsible for.
Action: the decision and the steps you took. This is most of the answer.
Result: a number, a user effect, or a before/after. If you lack a number, say what changed in the system.
Lesson: one sentence.
Two minutes. Then stop and let them pull a thread.
SDE-2 signals they are listening for: ownership, ambiguity, disagreement without contempt, a quality bar you enforced, cross-team work, a failure you changed something after.

cheats.title: What SDE-2 means
cheats.body:
You can take an ambiguous ticket, cut scope, write correct code, and land it without a daily design from someone else.
You can review other people's work and make it better.
You can design one service, including failure.
You can talk about a production problem you have seen, even if the production was a university project or a serious personal build. Do not invent a company you did not work at.
You are not expected to set multi-year technical strategy. That is the senior loop. Do not answer L4 questions with L6 architecture tourism.

cheats.title: A week on this desk
cheats.body:
Set a start date. Week 0 only if the language is not fluent.
Weekdays: do today's row. If you have 60 minutes, do the 60-minute column and mark the day Light. If you have two hours, do the plan as written. If you have three, do the stretch column.
If yesterday is unfinished, finish yesterday's 60-minute cut before starting a new pattern.
Sunday is review and stories. Do not add a new pattern on Sunday.
From Week 7, a mock replaces a study block. The retro is the deliverable.
From Week 12, the project repo is the AI deliverable. Notes without code do not count.
Mark status in the Daily Plan sheet. Confidence 1 or 2 means the next session starts by redoing that row, not by skipping ahead.

stories.signal: You can go deep on a design or a bug without hand-waving.

stories.prompt: A production incident or a serious project failure
stories.signal: You stay steady, communicate, and change the system afterward.
You can conflict without contempt and land a decision.
You make a reasonable assumption, check it, and adjust.

stories.prompt: Raising the quality bar on someone else's work
stories.signal: SDE-2 is not only your own tickets.
You do not externalize blame. Something changed because of the miss.
You influenced people who did not report to you.
You can point at a person whose day got better.
Initiative, scoped so you did not create chaos.
You cut scope on purpose and refused to cut the part that would have been reckless.
